author: Medical Xpress

title: Mayo transplant cardiologist outlines new detection and treatment advances for heart failure
content: Heart failure, a frequent complication of heart conditions, occurs when the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body’s needs, producing various symptoms. Cardiovascular diseases, which include heart failure, are the leading cause of death worldwide. Transplant cardiologist Jose Nativi Nicolau, M.D., of the Mayo Clinic in Florida, outlines recent advances in earlier detection and new treatment options for the condition.
summary: Heart failure is a common complication of heart conditions and occurs when the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs. Transplant cardiologist Jose Nativi Nicolau of the Mayo Clinic in Florida describes advances in detection and treatment for heart failure.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Tumor architecture and heterogeneity shape colorectal cancer progression and therapy
content: Tumor architecture in colorectal cancer is highly heterogeneous, with cancer cells from the same patient exhibiting markedly different characteristics and behaviors. This tumor heterogeneity diminishes therapeutic efficacy, as cells in distinct states may respond variably to treatment interventions.
summary: Tumors exhibit significant heterogeneity, with cancer cells in a single patient showing markedly different characteristics and behaviors. This heterogeneity lowers therapeutic efficacy because cells in different states may respond differently to treatments.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Sisters first to receive repurposed drug for rare blood disorder after genomic sequencing
content: Sisters who share a rare blood disorder have become the first patients to be treated with a repurposed medication. A team of doctors and cardiovascular scientists identified the drug’s target through genomic sequencing, enabling the new therapy for the condition.
summary: Sisters first to receive repurposed drug for rare blood disorder after genomic sequencing.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Young hikers in Peak District and Leicester find friendship in walking groups
content: Young hikers are sharing how participation in walking groups has improved their wellbeing. The discussion spans outings from the Peak District hills to Leicester’s city parks, featuring several young participants who say joining these groups has helped them feel better.
summary: Several young people have joined walking groups that hike in the Peak District hills and explore city parks of Leicester. They say the groups help them feel better.
author: BBC Health

title: Scientists discover most distant quasar formed 630 million years after Big Bang
content: Scientists have identified the most distant quasar yet, a galaxy core whose black hole is accreting material slowly. The quasar dates to roughly 630 million years after the Big Bang, placing it near the universe’s dawn and setting a new record for earliest‑formed quasars.
summary: Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet. The quasar’s galaxy core hosts a slow-chomping black hole and dates to about 630 million years after the Big Bang.
author: Phys.org

title: Study reveals two amino acid transport mechanisms in rare disease protein
content:
Research has identified two distinct mechanisms by which a protein associated with a rare disease transports amino acids. The findings add detail to the understanding of how this particular protein moves amino acids across cellular membranes.  

Cells continuously exchange amino acids with their surroundings using specialized membrane transporters, a process essential for protein synthesis and many physiological functions.
summary: Researchers identified two mechanisms by which a rare disease-associated protein transports amino acids. Cells rely on membrane transporters to exchange amino acids with their environment for protein synthesis and other processes.
author: Phys.org

title: Learning facts from interest may require less mental effort than learning for money
content: Research suggests that learning facts out of interest may require less mental effort than learning them for money. The source notes that humans can be motivated intrinsically—doing something because it is interesting or enjoyable—or extrinsically—doing it to obtain a reward such as money, praise or a good grade.
summary: Learning facts out of interest may require less mental effort than learning them for money. Intrinsic motivation is doing something because it is interesting or enjoyable, while extrinsic motivation is doing it to obtain a reward such as money, praise or a good grade.
author: Phys.org

title: Iron law of oligarchy first proposed by Robert Michels in early 1900s
content: The “iron law of oligarchy,” a concept first articulated by sociologist Robert Michels in the early 1900s, asserts that over a sufficient period any group will inevitably come to be governed by a small minority. This idea has lingered for more than a century as a pessimistic challenge to democratic ideals.
summary: The iron law of oligarchy suggests that over time every group ends up ruled by a few. The concept was first introduced by sociologist Robert Michels in the early 1900s.
author: Phys.org

title: St. Jude scientists redesign protein to boost DNA insertion by CASTs
content:
Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital have identified the mechanisms enabling precise DNA integration into specific genomic locations using CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs). By investigating type I-F3 CAST, the team uncovered structural details that explain how this protein family successfully inserts DNA at precise target sites. These findings provide new insights for future genomic engineering approaches.

The research, which highlights the potential of genome engineering to treat and cure diseases, was published in Nature. The study offers a clearer understanding of how molecular machinery selects targets, contributing to the ongoing development of biomedical innovations in this largely uncharted field.
summary: Researchers at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital demonstrated that protein redesign increases DNA insertion activity of type I‑F3 CRISPR‑associated transposases. Their structural analysis explains how the CAST machinery selects precise genomic targets and offers insights for future genome‑engineering approaches, with the findings published in Nature.
author: Phys.org

title: UN says global maritime trade to see zero growth in 2026
content: The United Nations said Thursday that global maritime trade, which transports more than 80 % of the world’s goods, is expected to show zero growth in 2026. The stagnation is attributed to shipping disruptions and trade uncertainties linked to the war in the Middle East.
summary: Global maritime trade, which moves more than 80% of the world’s goods, is projected to stagnate in 2026. The United Nations linked the zero‑growth outlook to shipping disruptions and trade uncertainties arising from the war in the Middle East, according to a Thursday statement.
author: Phys.org

title: Molecular cage catalysts vary over 10,000‑fold in activity, researchers find
content: Chemistry researchers have developed a new way to identify and understand highly effective artificial enzyme-like catalysts using powerful "molecular cages" that mimic the behavior of nature's enzymes. These tiny, hollow molecular structures act like miniature reaction chambers to trap molecules and accelerate chemical reactions. The cages showed enormous differences in performance, with the best catalysts more than 10,000 times more active than the least effective ones.
summary: Chemistry researchers have developed a new way to identify and understand highly effective artificial enzyme-like catalysts using powerful "molecular cages" that mimic the behavior of nature's enzymes. These tiny, hollow molecular structures act like miniature reaction chambers to trap molecules and accelerate chemical reactions.
author: Phys.org

title: University of Bayreuth creates digital edition platform for German lute tablature
content:
German lute tablature, a notation that can appear to modern readers as a secret code, was developed specifically for the Renaissance lute and preserves dances, songs and other musical works popular roughly 500 years ago. This rich notational tradition provides access to a fascinating world of historical music.

Researchers at the University of Bayreuth, working within an interdisciplinary team of experts, are using a digital scholarly‑edition platform to render these lute‑tablature sources both readable and audible once again.
summary: German lute tablature is a Renaissance notation that preserves dances, songs and other works popular about 500 years ago. Researchers at the University of Bayreuth, working in an interdisciplinary team, are using a digital scholarly edition platform to make these sources readable and audible again.
author: Phys.org

title: Author releases “Learning to Play Vim” manual after four years of work
content:
A developer announced the release of a new book titled Learning to Play Vim. The author, who began using Vim more than ten years ago, created the manual to provide a step‑by‑step guide that starts with basic concepts and progresses to advanced features. After more than four years of work—reported as 2,987 focused pomodoros, equivalent to 1,244 hours—the book was completed and made publicly available.

The manual is organized into 21 chapters and includes 170 exercises with solutions, along with real‑life examples that demonstrate how Vim can be configured for individual needs. Each topic references the related Vim help pages for further reading. Configuration examples are provided in both Vimscript and Lua, catering to users of Vim and Neovim, while explicitly avoiding Neovim‑specific features such as treesitter or LSP.

A landing page for the book is hosted at https://themouseless.Dev/vim/, and a sample containing the full table of contents and the first three chapters can be viewed at https://themouseless.Dev/content/learning_to_play_vim_sample.... The announcement was posted as a Show HN entry on Hacker News, receiving 82 points and 25 comments.
summary: The author announced the release of a new book titled Learning to Play Vim, which took more than four years and 2987 focused pomodoros (1244 hours) to write. The book includes 21 chapters, 170 exercises with solutions, real‑life examples, and configurations in both Vimscript and Lua, covering common Vim and Neovim features.
author: Hacker News

title: Kuwait intercepts Iranian drones, injuring four, and diverts passenger flights
content:
Kuwait's military reported four injuries after detecting and intercepting hostile Iranian drones in its airspace.

In response, flights crossing Iraq toward the Gulf were given new headings ahead of Kuwait, shifting the international corridor.
summary: Kuwait's military said four people were injured after a number of hostile Iranian drones were detected and intercepted in its airspace. Flights crossing Iraq toward the Gulf were given new headings ahead of Kuwait, shifting the international corridor.
author: Euronews

title: Russia launches missile and drone barrage on Ukraine, killing at least three
content: Russia launched a ballistic missile and a barrage of drones against Ukraine, killing at least three people. Ukraine’s air defences intercepted 87 Russian missiles and drones overnight on Thursday. In a separate action, Ukrainian drones hit a chemical plant that produces components for military explosives and a power station in the Stavropol region.
summary: Russia launched a ballistic missile and drone barrage on Ukraine that killed at least three people. Ukraine’s air defenses downed 87 Russian missiles and drones overnight, while Ukrainian drones struck a chemical plant and a power station in the Stavropol region.
author: Euronews

title: Diesel Tanker Capsizes off Ibiza, One Crew Member Killed, 17 Rescued
content: A tanker carrying about 7,000 tonnes of diesel capsized off Ibiza, prompting Spanish authorities to assess the risk of marine pollution. All 17 crew members were rescued, but one crew member died.
summary: A tanker carrying around 7,000 tonnes of diesel capsized off Ibiza. One crew member died, all 17 people on board were rescued, and Spanish authorities are assessing the risk of marine pollution.
author: Euronews

title: Peter Lochbihler urges EU to prioritize lesser-known tourism destinations
content: Peter Lochbihler of Booking.com argues that tourism should occupy a central position in European policymaking in an opinion piece for Euronews. He calls on the EU to support lesser‑known destinations, encouraging them to attract visitors worldwide and thereby fostering local revitalisation, growth and prosperity.
summary: Peter Lochbihler of Booking.com argues tourism should have a central place in European policymaking in an Euronews opinion piece. He says the EU should support lesser‑known destinations to attract visitors worldwide and foster local revitalisation, growth and prosperity.
author: Euronews

title: Iraq courts sentence eight French nationals to life for joining Islamic State
content: Iraqi courts have sentenced eight French nationals to life imprisonment for joining the Islamic State. In the same proceedings, two other French citizens received 15‑year prison terms, and the court postponed verdicts for an additional ten French nationals.
summary: Iraq sentenced eight French nationals to life imprisonment for joining Islamic State. Two French citizens were sentenced to 15 years in prison, and the verdict for ten additional French nationals was postponed.
author: Euronews

title: Germany's Christmas markets open nationwide with heightened security
content:
Christmas markets across Germany are open, welcoming visitors with dazzling lights, traditional treats and festive attractions.  

Security remains a priority following deadly attacks in recent years.
summary: Christmas markets across Germany are open, offering dazzling lights, traditional treats and festive attractions to visitors. Security remains a priority after deadly attacks in recent years.
author: Euronews

title: Marie‑Antoinette’s porcelain ‘nipple bowl’ fetches record $3.1 million at Paris auction
content:
The porcelain nipple bowl, known as a jatte‑teton, sold for a record €2.9 million ($3.1 million) at a Paris auction on Thursday.  
The bowl, once owned by Queen Marie‑Antoinette, was one of four pieces ordered by King Louis XVI for her royal dairy creamery.
summary: Marie‑Antoinette’s porcelain ‘nipple bowl’ fetches record $3.1 million at Paris auction.
author: France 24

title: Nigeria Faces Rising Election Violence Ahead of Presidential Vote
content:
In tonight’s edition, officials warned that rising electoral violence could deter voters from participating in Nigeria’s presidential election scheduled for January.  

Egyptian authorities have detained the driver of a car suspected of causing a fuel tanker to overturn on a major highway.  

Sierra Leone, previously labeled the world’s most dangerous place to give birth, now reports a dramatic drop in maternal deaths.
summary: Concerns are mounting that electoral violence could deter voters from taking part in Nigeria’s presidential election in January. The potential violence may impact voter participation in the January election.
author: France 24

title: Pablo Hernandez de Cos nominated as next European Central Bank president
content:
European leaders have agreed to nominate Pablo Hernandez de Cos, former head of the Bank of Spain, as the next president of the European Central Bank, replacing Christine Lagarde. The bank faces pressure to tackle high inflation, borrowing costs, and government debt.

Also in the show, US regulators gave SpaceX the green light to send satellites for data centers into space, and American households face higher costs for their Thanksgiving celebrations.
summary: European leaders agreed to nominate Pablo Hernandez de Cos, former head of the Bank of Spain, as the next president of the European Central Bank. He will replace outgoing Christine Lagarde as the bank confronts high inflation, borrowing costs and government debt.
author: France 24

title: Spain heads to general election as citizens express anger over government and establishment
content:
Three party leaders will compete in Spain’s general election on Sunday, an election called by left‑wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez after a parliamentary setback over housing legislation highlighted the fragility of his minority coalition government.  

In an interview with France 24’s Sharon Gaffney, Javier Carbonell, a policy analyst at the European Policy Centre, noted that despite solid economic growth, the Spanish population has suffered a housing crisis and inflation. He said citizens remain angry with the government and the economic system, and that ultimately they are angry with the establishment—Sanchez in this case—though he expects anger to shift toward PP and Vox soon.
summary: Spain heads to general election as citizens express anger over government and establishment.
author: France 24

title: Spain's snap election faces viral rigging claims, experts say they misrepresent system
content: Ahead of Spain's snap election on Sunday, allegations of vote rigging - known in Spanish as "pucherazo" - are spreading widely on social media. From claims that undocumented migrants are being illegally registered to vote, to allegations that postal ballots and vote counts could be manipulated, internet users are accusing Pedro Sánchez's government of attempting to rig the election. But these claims misrepresent how Spain's electoral system works, as Vedika Bahl explains in Truth or Fake.
summary: Spain's snap election faces viral rigging claims, experts say they misrepresent system.
author: France 24

title: RN faces new antisemitism claims; Le Pen may distance from Bardella
content: Could new allegations of antisemitism damage Jordan Bardella’s standing and the far-right National Rally’s electoral prospects? Charli James is pleased to welcome Paul Smith, Associate Professor in French and Francophone Studies at the University of Nottingham. Smith examines the far-right leader’s continued denials and considers whether Marine Le Pen might eventually distance herself from him. In the meantime, Smith suggests that Bardella needs to “make his mind up” about how to respond to these latest troubling allegations published by Le Monde and Mediapart. “It’s very difficult to deny. Le Monde and Mediapart, certainly Le Monde, wouldn’t be publishing these details if they didn’t have some pretty substantial evidence.” Could this prove to be the Achilles’ heel of a far-right party with its sights set on the second round of the presidential election?
summary: New antisemitism allegations published by Le Monde and Mediapart could damage Jordan Bardella’s standing and the National Rally’s electoral prospects. Associate Professor Paul Smith said the evidence appears substantial and suggested Marine Le Pen might eventually distance herself from Bardella.
author: France 24

title: Expert links Black Friday hype to shoppers' desire for collective experience
content:
Black Friday, once limited to the United States, is now described as a truly global retail phenomenon, drawing shoppers from places such as Louisiana in the United States to queues outside stores in Venezuela. The day has become the largest occasion of the year for retail foot traffic.

In a FRANCE 24 interview, host Sharon Gaffney spoke with Olaya Moldes Andres, an Associate Professor in Marketing and Strategy at Cardiff Business School. Andres said that, beyond the appeal of discounts, the event’s popularity may stem from shoppers’ desire to “join the collective action.” She noted that participating—whether by spending money or visiting malls—makes people feel part of a shared experience, likening the motivation to that behind Christmas or other social events.
summary: Black Friday has expanded from a US-only event to a global phenomenon and is the biggest day of the year for retail foot traffic. Olaya Moldes Andres, Associate Professor in Marketing and Strategy at Cardiff Business School, said the hype may stem from shoppers wanting to feel part of a collective event.
author: France 24

title: Pablo Hernández de Cos chosen as next ECB president, first Spaniard
content: Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos, a former governor of the Bank of Spain, has been selected to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank. The appointment follows his securing of support from the European Union’s largest member states. Hernández de Cos will become the first Spaniard to head the ECB, overtaking rival candidate Klaas Knot, who previously led the Dutch central bank. The decision marks a transition in the bloc’s monetary‑policy leadership.
summary: Former Bank of Spain governor Pablo Hernández de Cos has been selected to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank. He became the first Spaniard to lead the ECB after winning support from the EU’s biggest countries and defeating rival Klaas Knot, the former head of the Dutch central bank.
author: Guardian World

title: EU leaders wrestle over Ukraine aid as potential Le Pen victory sparks fear
content:
EU leaders are confronting a split over a €45 billion loan for Ukraine that is slated for 2027. Slovakia, Hungary and Czechia have signaled a desire to opt out of the financing, while the bloc works to complete its budget negotiations before year‑end.  

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Brussels on Thursday and urged that all 27 member states back the loan, stressing that EU funding must be provided by the whole Union, not a reduced group. He added that Germany is seeking to safeguard the aid amid concerns about a possible far‑right French presidency.
summary: EU leaders wrestle over Ukraine aid as potential Le Pen victory sparks fear.
author: Guardian World

title: Sam Wood denied bail, will spend Christmas in jail over alleged assault of wife
content:
Former Bachelor star and fitness influencer Sam Wood is accused of assaulting his wife, Snezana, while the family was holidaying at Noosa on the Sunshine Coast in October. The domestic‑violence charges allege that Wood strangled and assaulted his wife during the trip.

A court of appeal heard Wood’s third bail application on the day and again denied bail, meaning he will remain in custody and spend Christmas in jail. Wood, 46, has been in custody for eight weeks since his arrest.
summary: Reality star Sam Wood was denied bail on domestic violence charges alleging he strangled and assaulted his wife, Snezana, during a family holiday at Noosa in Queensland in October. He has been in custody for eight weeks and will remain in jail over the Christmas period.
author: Guardian World

title: Qantas and Air New Zealand planes too close at Sydney airport as ‘mental models’ of crews to be investigated
content:
The Australian Transport Safety Bureau has opened an investigation into flight crews’ “mental models” after a series of incidents in which Qantas and Air New Zealand aircraft were reported to have been too close to each other at Sydney Airport. The probe will examine how pilots perceive and respond to other traffic during approach and landing phases.

One of the incidents involved Qantas flight 426, a Boeing 737 operating from Melbourne. The aircraft was due to land just before 10:15 a.m. on Wednesday when the crew aborted the descent after spotting another aircraft crossing the runway, having been advised to expect a late landing clearance.
summary: Qantas and Air New Zealand planes too close at Sydney airport as ‘mental models’ of crews to be investigated.
author: Guardian World

title: Bushfire on Flinders Island worsens as Australia braces for heatwaves, floods and storms
content:
Major weather extremes are forecast across Australia from Friday into the weekend, including heatwaves, severe storms, heavy rain, floods and major fires. Firefighters are battling an out‑of‑control bushfire on Flinders Island, where authorities said at least eight buildings have been destroyed or significantly damaged and conditions are expected to worsen on Friday.

In Victoria, storms forecast for the east coast mean a wet and windy day for voters on election day. The combined threats highlight a period of heightened weather risk nationwide.
summary: Firefighters are battling an out‑of‑control bushfire on Flinders Island, where authorities say at least eight buildings have been destroyed or significantly damaged. Weather forecasts call for heatwaves, floods, severe storms and heavy rain across Australia from Friday into the weekend.
author: Guardian World

title: China interference threatens Taiwan's local elections, officials warn
content:
Taiwanese officials have warned that China could interfere in the upcoming local elections, a concern that underscores the political stakes for the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP). The elections, held every four years, will determine mayors, council members and other local leaders in 22 districts across the island.

Unlike presidential contests that hinge on foreign‑policy debates, these local contests focus on everyday matters such as housing affordability and wealth distribution. The results will shape the DPP’s prospects as it navigates an increasingly precarious set of relationships on the global stage.
summary: Taiwanese officials say China is interfering in the local elections that will shape the fortunes of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party. Voters on Saturday will elect mayors, council members and other local leaders in 22 districts, with the contests focusing on issues such as housing affordability and wealth distribution.
author: Guardian World

title: New Zealand coalition must partner with Opportunity party to form government
content:
The final count of New Zealand’s general election shows the incumbent right‑wing coalition lacking a majority and requiring the backing of the centrist newcomer Opportunity party to form a government and avoid a further election. Incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon has lost his majority and must secure that support to remain in power.

Preliminary results released on 7 November gave the National party and its two partners – the populist New Zealand First and the libertarian Act party – a slim two‑seat lead, leaving the outcome too close to call until the final votes were tallied.
summary: Incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon lost his majority and will need the support of the centrist Opportunity party to stay in power. The final results show the National party, New Zealand First and Act parties hold only a slim two‑seat lead, making the coalition dependent on the newcomer party to avoid another election.
author: Guardian World

title: HBO Max Black Friday Deal Offers Dune Content for $5.49 Monthly
content:
The HBO Max Amazon Prime Video add-on is available at a discounted rate of $5.49 per month for 12 months, down from the standard price of $10.99. This Black Friday deal allows subscribers to stream the Dune franchise, including Dune: Part 1 and Dune: Part 2, as well as the prequel series Dune: Prophecy. The promotion is designed for viewers looking to catch up on the sci-fi saga before the release of Dune: Part 3, which arrives on December 18.

To utilize this offer, users must have an Amazon account, though an Amazon Prime subscription is not required. The deal includes the HBO Max Basic plan, which provides access to a wide range of content, including DC Comics properties, crime dramas, and various science fiction titles. After the initial 12-month period, the monthly price will revert to $10.99. Subscribers can cancel the service at any time.

The HBO Max library features a variety of titles beyond the Dune movies. Notable sci-fi content includes Scavengers Reign, Station Eleven, Mickey 17, and 2001: A Space Odyssey. The platform also hosts the DC Comics universe, ranging from the 1978 Superman film to recent movies by James Gunn. Additionally, the service offers classic television series such as The Sopranos and the David Lynch-directed 1984 Dune film.

The Basic plan includes 1080P video quality and contains advertisements; 4K resolution is exclusive to the HBO Max Premium tier. Dune: Prophecy is noted as essential viewing for fans, set years before the events of the Legendary Pictures films. The article ranks both HBO Max and Amazon Prime as top streaming services for sci-fi enthusiasts, suggesting that combining the two offers broad coverage of the genre.

This discount is described as one of the best deals seen in recent times, with previous offers typically providing around 40% off. The promotion is part of a broader range of Black Friday deals, which also include electronics, toys, and other streaming services. The article advises that this offer is particularly suitable for fans of science fiction and superheroes who want a diverse library to entertain family members with non-sci-fi content.
summary: HBO Max Black Friday Deal Offers Dune Content for $5.49 Monthly.
author: Space.com

title: Dwarflab Dwarf Mini Smart Telescope Now $339 for Black Friday, 19% Off
content:
The Dwarflab Dwarf Mini is a pocket‑sized smart telescope that has been promoted as a “portable smart telescope” capable of photographing deep‑sky objects such as nebulas, galaxies, star clusters, and even the Sun in its solar mode.  The device is marketed as being small enough to fit in a backpack, weighing only 1.8 lb (840 g) and featuring a built‑in solar filter.  Its compact form factor is highlighted as a key advantage for users who travel to dark‑sky sites or who live in light‑polluted urban areas.

According to the review, the Dwarf Mini is easy to set up and automatically finds and tracks targets, with the resulting image displayed on a connected smartphone or tablet.  The review, written by Jamie Carter, awarded the telescope four out of five stars for its simple operation and the quality of its astrophotography.  The 2 MP sensor produces images that are best suited for sharing on smartphones, and the telescope includes a mosaic mode that allows users to capture a larger portion of the sky without stitching separate frames together.

The product was launched in January 2026 and is now being sold at its lowest‑ever price.  The original price of $419 has been reduced by $80 for the Black Friday sale, bringing the current price to $339 on Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart.  The sale has already attracted a 50 % purchase rate on Amazon.  The Dwarf Mini’s specifications include a 180‑inch (30 mm) aperture, 150 mm focal length, a field of view of 50.59 × 45.06 degrees (wide) or 2.5 × 2.14 degrees (telephoto), and dimensions of 7.24 in × 3.94 in × 2.4 in.  It also offers 64 GB of storage, a 7 000 mAh battery lasting about four hours, and an Alt‑Az/EQ mount.

Space+ members can join the platform for free and automatically enter a prize draw to win one of two Dwarf Mini telescopes.  The article notes that the device is best suited for users who value portability and ease of use, while those seeking higher‑resolution imaging may prefer a different model such as the ZWO Seestar S50 Pro.
summary: The Dwarflab Dwarf Mini smart telescope is now available on Amazon for $339, down $80 from its original $419 price for Black Friday. It weighs 1.8 lbs, has a 30 mm aperture, and can photograph nebulas, galaxies, star clusters, and the Sun in solar mode, with automatic target tracking displayed on a smartphone screen.
author: Space.com

title: Smart Telescopes Under $700 for Black Friday: Full Deal List
content:
Smart telescopes let users point, focus, and photograph their favorite night‑sky targets with only a few minutes of setup and a single button press. After years of reviewing many models, the review team now recommends only a handful as the best options. Prices range from a few hundred dollars to several thousand, so the article highlights three models that are already under $700 before Black Friday deals, and it also lists premium models that offer significant savings for those willing to pay more.

For those unsure about purchasing, the review invites readers to join Space+, the membership community, which includes a prize draw to win the highly portable Dwarf Mini smart telescope. The Dwarf Mini was originally priced at $419 and is now $339.15. The review gave it four stars and praised its suitability for beginners and for convenient, on‑the‑go astrophotography.

Other highlighted deals include the ZWO Seestar S30 Plus, which saves $25. It is recommended for beginners because of its excellent deep‑sky imaging, low cost, and built‑in filters for dual‑band nebulas and solar observation. The ZWO Seestar S30 Pro saves $35, features an 8.3‑megapixel sensor, and performs well under light‑polluted skies, making it ideal for imaging galaxies and nebulas.

A savings of over $500 is available on a versatile smart telescope that is small, lightweight, and comes with autofocus and no collimation requirement. The review awarded it four and a half stars in the Unistellar Odyssey review, noting its great views of deep‑space objects and good color rendition in astrophotography shots.

Finally, the Vespera Pro 2, originally $2,990, is now $2,490. This premium motorized telescope includes a 12.5‑megapixel sensor, an upgraded optical design over the Vaonis Vespera Pro, a mosaic mode for stitching wider portions of the night sky, and a tall carbon‑fiber tripod that is ready for use out of the box.
summary: The article lists several smart telescopes under $700 that are good for beginners, including the Dwarf Mini, ZWO Seestar S30 Plus, and ZWO Seestar S30 Pro, all of which have Black Friday discounts. It also highlights higher‑end models like the Unistellar Odyssey and Vespera Pro 2, which offer advanced features and significant savings.
author: Space.com

title: Aperture Kids' 'Between the Balloons' honors Macy's Parade 100th anniversary
content: Between the Balloons: My Thanksgiving Parade is the first book from Aperture Kids, which aims to create community and understanding through photography. The book celebrates the historic 100th anniversary of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade with images by EA Kahane, illustrations by The New Yorker cartoonist Tom Toro and a story by Doro Globus
summary: Between the Balloons: My Thanksgiving Parade is the first book from Aperture Kids. The book celebrates the historic 100th anniversary of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade with images by EA Kahane, illustrations by New Yorker cartoonist Tom Toro, and a story by Doro Globus.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Former England scrum-half Nigel Starmer-Smith dies at 81
content: Former England scrum-half and broadcaster Nigel Starmer-Smith has died at the age of 81, according to an announcement by his family. He made seven appearances for England between 1969 and 1971, and also played for Harlequins and the Barbarians. Additionally, Starmer-Smith presented the BBC program Rugby Special for 15 years.
summary: Former England scrum-half and broadcaster Nigel Starmer-Smith has died at the age of 81, his family announced. He made seven appearances for England between 1969 and 1971 and presented Rugby Special on the BBC for 15 years.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Sindarov Survives Near Sudden Death, Splits Point with Gukesh in 60‑Move Match
content:
The world chess championship match between India’s Gukesh Dommaraju and Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov ended in a draw on Thursday, leveling the contest at 1½–1½ ahead of the first rest day. The game, which lasted nearly five hours, saw Sindarov come within eight seconds of sudden defeat before fighting back to split the point. This third consecutive draw follows two quieter previous games, marking a significant increase in tension for the $2.5 million match.

Played at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in the Geneva suburbs, the 60-move battle featured Gukesh, playing with the black pieces, returning to the Berlin defense of the Ruy Lopez. Gukesh introduced an early surprise on move five by developing his bishop, which placed Sindarov behind on the clock for the first time in the match. By move 15, Gukesh retained nearly 1 hour and 58 minutes of his starting two hours, holding a significant time advantage of almost 40 minutes over the challenger.
summary: Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov came within eight seconds of sudden death before fighting back to split the point with India’s Gukesh Dommaraju in a 60‑move match at the Fondation Martin Bodmer. The game left the world title match tied 1½–1½ heading into the first rest day.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Jannik Sinner ruled out of Australian Open after knee surgery
content:
Organizers have confirmed that two-time Australian Open champion Jannik Sinner will not compete at the Melbourne Park grand slam in January due to a persistent knee injury. The World No. 2 underwent a minor operation on Tuesday, according to his own statement.

Italian sports daily Corriere dello Sport reports that Sinner faces up to four months of recovery from the surgery. This injury extends his long absence from the tour, as the last time he competed was at Wimbledon in July.
summary: Jannik Sinner, the two‑time Australian Open champion, has been ruled out of the January grand slam at Melbourne Park after surgery on a persistent knee injury. The organisers said he will be out for up to four months following a minor operation, extending his long absence from the tour after last playing Wimbledon in July.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Nations Championship Finals See Woolly Hats, Thermal Vests and Low Ticket Sales
content:
The Nations Championship finals weekend is shaping up to be a test of the event’s future viability, with players and coaches taking the opportunity to unwind after the season’s grind. While organisers are cautious about calling the weekend the “Glastonbury of Rugby” at this stage, the festival‑style atmosphere is evident.

Forecast temperatures of 3 °C mean that thermal vests and woolly hats will be more common than at Worthy Farm in June, and even Cher would need to bundle up if she were to appear. The cooler weather is expected to influence the overall look of the crowd.

At Allianz Stadium, the moshpit will have noticeable gaps during the Italy‑Fiji and Ireland‑Australia kick‑offs, as the three‑day finals extravaganza unfolds beneath the Friday night lights. Organisers have admitted that Friday has been a challenge in terms of ticket sales, a situation that does not yet account for rush‑hour traffic and public transport disruption.
summary: The Nations Championship finals weekend featured players and coaches letting loose amid 3°C temperatures, leading to widespread use of woolly hats and thermal vests. Organisers reported Friday as a challenge in ticket sales, with gaps in the Allianz Stadium moshpit during Italy vs Fiji and Ireland vs Australia matches.
author: Guardian Sport

title: George Russell Says Max Verstappen Feud Was 'Quite Amusing'
content:
George Russell has stated he has no desire to continue his feud with Max Verstappen, describing the conflict as avoidable and unnecessary. However, the Mercedes driver confirmed he will not retract his comments from last week’s Las Vegas Grand Prix, where he criticized Verstappen following a practice session clash. Russell said, “I’m not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this.”

Verstappen previously dismissed the British driver, claiming Russell was “below my level” and expressing that he does not want poor relationships with people. Despite the ongoing tension, Russell characterized the situation as “quite amusing” while maintaining his stance on the incident in Nevada.
summary: George Russell Says Max Verstappen Feud Was 'Quite Amusing'.
author: Guardian Sport

title: FIFA Staff Invited to Congressional Interviews Over Infantino FFE Scandal
content:
A congressional probe into the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scandal has prompted the House Judiciary Committee to request testimony from both current and former Fifa staff. On Wednesday, letters were sent to a number of present employees and a handful of former senior personnel, asking them to attend interviews as part of the investigation.

The committee’s inquiries focus on Gianni Infantino’s alleged failed FFE scheme and potential connections between Fifa and the Trump administration. Democrats have indicated that Infantino could be subpoenaed to provide evidence as the investigation gains momentum.
summary: Past and present FIFA employees received letters requesting they attend interviews for a congressional investigation into the FIFA Forward Enterprise scandal. Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee have asked them to give evidence as they examine Gianni Infantino’s failed FFE scheme and links between FIFA and the Trump administration.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Éric Cantona Calls Himself a 'Flower of Evil' in New Documentary
content: Before the release of a new documentary, the unrepentant Manchester United icon reflects on his deep bond with English football and his darker instincts “I’m an angel and a demon,” Éric Cantona says intently during a gripping new documentary about his life on and off the football pitch. “And an angel or a demon, you love him or you hate him. I’m far from being the person with the greatest integrity. I’m far from being the person who always tells the truth. I’m far from being the person who has never been hypocritical. Maybe I’m a good person, but I can also be a flower of evil. It’s the first time in my life I’ve realised this. I am a flower of evil, and I find it very beautiful.” It’s hard to know what to expect from the only written interview pinned to the release of Cantona: Flower of Evil. Joel Cantona has warned that his famous brother will walk out at any mention of the enduring crisis surrounding Manchester United, whether it’s a question about Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival or the Glazer family’s ruinous ownership of the club.
summary: Éric Cantona calls himself a 'flower of evil' in a new documentary about his life on and off the football pitch. Joel Cantona has warned that his brother will walk out at any mention of the crisis surrounding Manchester United.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Great Britain reach Davis Cup semis after Patten, Skupski win decisive tie
content: Great Britain advanced to the Davis Cup semi‑finals for the first time since 2019 after winning a decisive doubles tie in Bologna. Henry Patten and Neal Skupski secured the victory against Germany, clinching the match and the team’s place in the next round.
summary: Great Britain advanced to the semi-finals of the Davis Cup for the first time since 2019. Henry Patten and Neal Skupski won a decisive doubles tie against Germany in Bologna.
author: BBC Sport

title: Taylor and Lewis Lose All Five Matches on Return to MODUS Super Series International Pairs
content: Phil Taylor and England teammate Adrian Lewis lost all five matches after returning to darts action together at the MODUS Super Series International Pairs tournament.
summary: Phil Taylor and his England team-mate Adrian Lewis lost all five matches after returning to darts action together at the MODUS Super Series International Pairs tournament. They had returned to competition together.
author: BBC Sport

title: George Russell calls Max Verstappen's post‑Vegas Grand Prix criticism 'quite amusing'
content: George Russell says Max Verstappen can "say what he wants" and that he found the Red Bull driver's criticisms of him after the Las Vegas Grand Prix "quite amusing".
summary: George Russell said Max Verstappen can say what he wants. He found Verstappen's criticisms after the Las Vegas Grand Prix quite amusing.
author: BBC Sport

title: FIFA confirms cyberattack stole limited personal and business information
content: FIFA, the international governing body for soccer, confirmed on Thursday that it was the victim of a criminal cyberattack. The incident resulted in unauthorized access and the theft of a limited set of personal and business information.
summary: FIFA stated on Thursday that it was the victim of a criminal cyberattack. The incident resulted in the unauthorized access and theft of a limited set of personal and business information.
author: The Hill

title: EPA: No airborne lead detected in Iowa after Army blast
content: The Environmental Protection Agency announced Thursday that its air monitors in southeastern Iowa detected no airborne lead after the Army’s controlled detonation of thousands of pounds of unstable explosives. The agency remains awaiting laboratory results from its environmental testing.
summary: The EPA reported that air monitors detected no airborne lead following an Army controlled detonation in southeastern Iowa. Administrator Lee Zeldin stated that the agency is still awaiting laboratory results from its environmental testing.
author: The Hill

title: Nearly 100 Labour MPs Oppose Rosebank Oil Field as Energy Secretary Prepares Decision
content: Nearly 100 Labour MPs, including ministerial aides, have expressed opposition to the Rosebank oil field. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is scheduled to decide within weeks whether to grant permission for drilling in the field off the north‑west coast of Shetland.
summary: Nearly 100 Labour MPs, including ministerial aides, oppose drilling at the Rosebank oil field. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is due to decide whether to grant a drilling go‑ahead off the north‑west coast of Shetland within weeks.
author: BBC Politics

title: Labour MP Catherine Fookes Organised Letter Urging Andy Burnham to Reject Rosebank
content:
Catherine Fookes, the Labour MP for Monmouthshire, has highlighted a letter from nearly 100 MPs that exposed a split within Labour over the Rosebank oilfield. The letter argues that approval of the project would be celebrated by oil giants, but it would not benefit constituents who are concerned about the climate crisis and rising energy bills.

The MP points out that millions of households are facing another winter of unaffordable energy costs, while this summer’s heatwaves were linked to more than 5,000 deaths across the UK. She stresses that the cost of living and the climate crisis are two sides of the same coin, with continued dependence on fossil fuels driving up bills, fuelling deadly extreme weather, and causing widespread harm.

Fookes recalls that a year ago, Storm Claudia’s floods swept through Monmouthshire, devastating hundreds of homes, businesses and livelihoods. As flood season returns, she notes how residents feel sick every time it rains.
summary: Labour MP Catherine Fookes organised a letter from nearly 100 MPs urging Andy Burnham to reject the Rosebank oilfield project. The letter argues that approving the project would benefit oil giants but would not help constituents who are concerned about climate change and rising energy bills.
author: Guardian Environment

title: World’s Rivers and Lakes Drop 5.7% and 9.5% in Record-Heat Years, Study Finds
content:
An international study led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences reports that extreme global heat caused an unprecedented decline in surface freshwater during 2023 and 2024, the two hottest years on record. The analysis found that global river flows fell to about 5.7 % below normal, while water stored in lakes and reservoirs dropped by 9.5 %. This combined drop represents the largest synchronized decline in surface water since at least 1991.  

The study notes that the effects were particularly pronounced in South America, where water levels plunged even as some areas experienced extreme rainfall.
summary: World’s Rivers and Lakes Drop 5.7% and 9.5% in Record-Heat Years, Study Finds.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Study suggests brain immune cells may weaken motor memories by removing myelin
content:
A recent study suggests that brain immune cells could weaken motor memories by removing myelin.  

Learning new movements strengthens connections between brain cells, while motor skill acquisition also triggers changes in myelin, an insulating material around nerve fibers produced by oligodendrocytes.
summary: The study suggests brain immune cells could weaken motor memories by removing myelin. Learning new movements strengthens some brain cell connections and also prompts changes in myelin produced by oligodendrocytes.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study finds heart cells may transmit electrical signals beyond direct connections
content: New evidence suggests that heart cells transmit electrical signals through mechanisms beyond direct connections. The heart can beat three billion times or more over a lifetime, continuing for 75 years or longer without conscious thought while a person sleeps, works or exercises.
summary: New evidence indicates heart cells can transmit electrical signals through mechanisms other than direct connections. The heart beats about 3 billion times over a lifespan of 75 years or more, operating continuously while a person sleeps, works or exercises.
author: Medical Xpress

title: UNIGE team discovers dual origin of ovarian cells via rete ovarii
content:
Ovaries develop, yet much remains unknown. A team at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) studied the “rete ovarii,” a small anatomical structure that has long been overlooked.

Their research uncovered the dual origin of the cells that surround and protect oocytes. The discovery offers new insights into ovarian development and opens new avenues for research into fertility and gynecological cancers.
summary: A team at the University of Geneva studied the rete ovarii, a small anatomical structure long overlooked, and found that the cells surrounding and protecting oocytes have a dual origin. The discovery provides new insights into ovarian development and may open new avenues for research into fertility and gynecological cancers.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Experimental drug PHI-101 shows promise against resistant FLT3-positive AML
content:
Researchers at Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center and Johns Hopkins Children's Center found an experimental drug may help overcome a major challenge in treating FLT3‑positive acute myeloid leukemia. In laboratory and animal studies, the drug, called PHI‑101, was effective against leukemia cells carrying genetic mutations that cause resistance to existing FLT3‑targeted therapies.  

The findings suggest PHI‑101 could address therapy resistance in patients with FLT3‑positive AML.
summary: Researchers at Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center and Johns Hopkins Children's Center found that experimental drug PHI-101 may help overcome treatment resistance in FLT3-positive acute myeloid leukemia. In laboratory and animal studies, PHI-101 was effective against leukemia cells with genetic mutations that cause resistance to existing FLT3-targeted therapies.
author: Medical Xpress

title: CNIO and Stanford researchers uncover new aspect of DNA duplication process
content:
A protein that teaches cells to tolerate DNA damage has been identified as pointing to a new vulnerability in cancer. The discovery, highlighted in the title, suggests that this protein’s role in cellular response to DNA damage could offer a therapeutic angle for cancer treatment.

Researchers at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre (CNIO) and Stanford University have uncovered a new aspect of DNA duplication, a process that remains poorly understood despite decades of study. DNA is copied every time a cell divides into two daughter cells, and the work at CNIO focuses on how this fundamental mechanism is linked to the origins of cancer.
summary: Researchers at CNIO and Stanford University have uncovered a new aspect of the DNA duplication process. The process, which has been studied for decades, still holds many surprises.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Oral nutrition supplements show short-term benefits and cost savings for older adults
content:
The systematic review, published in Value in Health by Amarsinh Desai, Ph.D., Olivia M. Dong, Ph.D., and colleagues, examined the health and economic effects of oral nutrition supplements in older adults, most of whom were with or at risk of malnutrition.

The researchers found that oral nutrition supplement use, often as part of broader nutrition interventions, was generally associated with modest short‑term improvements in health outcomes and was cost‑effective or cost‑saving. Economic benefits were largely driven by reductions in health‑care resource utilization, such as fewer hospitalizations.
summary: A systematic review published in the journal Value in Health by Amarsinh Desai, Ph. D., Olivia M.
author: Medical Xpress

title: New platform uncovers metabolic targets shaped by cancer mutations
content:
The study shows tumors rewire metabolism to divert nutrients into energy and raw materials for growth and division.  

Using a novel platform, the study reveals that different cancer‑causing mutations shape metabolism even within the same organ, pointing to new metabolic targets for cancer treatment.
summary: A new study shows that different cancer-causing mutations can shape metabolism within the same organ. The study highlights that tumors rewire metabolism to divert nutrients into energy and raw materials needed for growth.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Expert says treating obesity involves more than willpower, outlines options
content: The piece notes that deciding how to treat obesity can feel overwhelming because a range of options—diet plans, weight‑loss surgery, newer pills and weekly injections—are marketed as effective. It highlights the difficulty many people face in determining when and where to begin treatment.
summary: An expert explains that obesity treatment is not just a lack of willpower. Options such as diet plans, weight‑loss surgery, newer pills and weekly injections make it hard to know when to start.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Chief medical officer Gregor Smith resigns citing mental health concerns
content: Chief medical officer Gregor Smith, 55, announced his resignation, citing mental‑health reasons. Smith has held the post since December 2020 and, in recent weeks, has been questioned about his role in the handling of avoidable deaths at NHS Grampian.
summary: Gregor Smith, the 55-year-old chief medical officer who has held the post since December 2020, has resigned on mental health grounds. His resignation follows recent questions about his role in the handling of avoidable deaths at NHS Grampian.
author: BBC Health

title: God‑faced rings may have marked Mesoamerican long‑distance merchants
content: Over a millennium ago, a Mesoamerican traveler is described as arriving in foreign territory while displaying a hand‑wearing a ring that bore the face of a god. The ring’s purpose is uncertain, though the suggestion has been made that such “god‑faced” rings may have served to identify long‑distance merchants.
summary: Over 1,000 years ago a Mesoamerican traveler displayed a ring with a deity’s face when arriving in foreign lands. Researchers propose that such god‑faced rings may have been used to identify long‑distance merchants.
author: Phys.org

title: Spain moves to contain diesel spill after tanker capsizes off Ibiza, one dead
content: Spanish authorities moved quickly on Thursday to limit damage to Mediterranean waters after a tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes (7,700 tons) of diesel capsized off Ibiza. The accident left one person dead, prompting emergency response efforts to contain any potential oil spill.
summary: Spanish authorities raced to contain any damage to Mediterranean waters after a tanker capsized off Ibiza. The tanker was carrying up to 7,000 tonnes (7,700 tons) of diesel and the incident left one dead.
author: Phys.org

title: Thailand finds dangerous arsenic and lead levels in river shellfish
content: Thai authorities reported that tests on shellfish and other river species revealed dangerous levels of arsenic and lead. The contamination is linked to rivers affected by suspected mining pollution from neighboring Myanmar, an official said on Thursday.
summary: Thai authorities have found dangerous levels of arsenic and lead in shellfish and other river species. The contamination is linked to suspected mining pollution from neighboring Myanmar, an official said Thursday.
author: Phys.org

title: Researchers warn 5G leaks could disrupt satellite weather measurements
content: Researchers from New Jersey and Maryland, led by Behzad Golparvar of Rutgers University, warn that leaks from future 5G networks could interfere with satellite weather measurements and potentially alter high‑impact forecasts. Their concern centers on the possible impact of 5G emissions on weather‑satellite data.
summary: A group of researchers from New Jersey and Maryland is examining whether leaks from future 5G networks could interfere with satellite weather measurements. Lead author Behzad Golparvar of Rutgers University says the interference could potentially alter high‑impact weather forecasts.
author: Phys.org

title: Astronomers find runaway pulsar that escaped its supernova remnant
content: Astronomers have identified a rare pulsar that has moved beyond the debris cloud of the supernova that created it. The find, made by chance, was reported by a team led by Rohit Dokara, formerly of the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy, and joins only a few similar cases known to date.
summary: Astronomers have spotted a rare pulsar that has escaped the cloud of debris left by its own supernova explosion. The team, led by Rohit Dokara, formerly at the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy, made the discovery by chance, adding to only a handful of similar known cases.
author: Phys.org

title: Wave-like animal group displays may have evolved as predator deception, study says
content: In a Perspectives piece published in Science, Dr. Eduardo Sampaio of the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior (MPI‑AB) and professor Iain Couzin of the University of Konstanz argue that wave‑like displays in animal groups may have evolved as a form of deception. The authors note that when a predator approaches, some groups transform into striking, pulsing waves. They suggest these patterns are more than a side effect of group living, proposing that the visual effect could mislead or deter predators.
summary: Some animal groups form pulsing wave patterns when predators approach. Dr. Eduardo Sampaio and professor Iain Couzin argue these displays may have evolved as deception in a Perspectives piece published in Science.
author: Phys.org

title: DESTINY model uses Markov chains to simulate chemistry on icy interstellar dust grains
content: Astrophysicists at the University of Liège have introduced a deterministic approach to model molecular chemistry on the surfaces of tiny, ice-covered dust grains in interstellar space. This new method utilizes Markov chains with absorbing states, a mathematical tool that had not previously been applied in astrochemistry. The research aims to better represent the active chemical processes where molecules form on these uneven grain surfaces. The findings from this work are published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.
summary: Astrophysicists at the University of Liège have introduced a deterministic approach based on Markov chains with absorbing states to track molecular chemistry on uneven, ice‑covered interstellar dust grains. The model and its results are reported in a paper published in Astronomy & Astrophysics.
author: Phys.org

title: Trump admin approves Elon Musk's plan for one million SpaceX Starmind data satellites
content:
The Trump administration has approved Elon Musk’s proposal to establish datacentres in space. US federal regulators authorized the launch of one million Starmind orbital satellites, manufactured by SpaceX, to process data off-Earth. Proponents of the initiative contend that this approach will enhance energy efficiency and mitigate the environmental footprint of terrestrial datacentres as the artificial intelligence sector expands.

The Guardian’s global technology editor, Dan Milmo, discusses the feasibility of this plan and its potential implications in an interview with Michael Safi. The conversation addresses the realistic prospects of deploying such a massive satellite network for data processing purposes.
summary: The Trump administration approved Elon Musk’s plan to create space‑based datacentres, authorising the launch of one million Starmind orbital satellites built by SpaceX. Supporters say the project could be more energy‑efficient and lower the environmental impact of Earth‑based datacentres as the AI industry expands.
author: Guardian Science

title: Hormonal contraceptive use drops sharply in Great Britain over past decade, study says
content: Survey published in Lancet reveals ‘hormonal hesitancy’ on the rise – with implants and injections also increasingly spurned The number of young women using hormonal contraception fell drastically in the past decade, with social media fuelling the “hormonal hesitancy” phenomenon. New findings from the fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-4), published in The Lancet, found that almost one in five women in Great Britain at risk of unintended pregnancy were not using effective contraception.
summary: Hormonal contraceptive use drops sharply in Great Britain over past decade, study says.
author: Guardian Science

title: Sex among British adults drops, under‑45s have half the monthly encounters of 1990
content:
Sex among British adults has declined sharply in recent decades.  Under‑45s now report half as many monthly sexual encounters as they did in 1990, and one in three people under 25 say they have never had sexual intercourse.  

In a video interview, science editor and co‑host Ian Sample discusses these trends with Madeleine Finlay.  Sample explains why young people might be postponing sex and explores factors that could be driving the notable increase in women who say they do not want children.
summary: Sex among British adults has slumped in recent decades, with under-45s having half as many monthly encounters as in 1990 and one in three under-25s reporting that they have never had sexual intercourse. To unpick some of the possible reasons behind these declines, Madeleine Finlay hears from science editor and co-host Ian Sample.
author: Guardian Science

title: Tell HN post wishes Happy Thanksgiving
content: A user posted a brief note on Hacker News wishing readers a Happy Thanksgiving. The message encourages people to spend the holiday with friends and family, and if circumstances are less than ideal, to make the day enjoyable anyway. The comment has garnered 526 points and 130 comments.
summary: The Tell HN post titled Happy Thanksgiving hopes readers have a great day with friends and family. The post has received 526 points and 130 comments on Hacker News.
author: Hacker News

title: SimDrop adds running iOS simulators to macOS Finder sidebar
content:
A developer announced SimDrop, a macOS utility designed to streamline iOS‑simulator workflows. The tool places each running iOS simulator in the Finder sidebar under Locations, exposing two folders for each simulator: a Downloads folder (corresponding to Files app → On My iPhone → Downloads) and a Photos and Videos folder (the simulator’s Photos library). Simulators are added to the sidebar when they boot and removed when they shut down, and the same directories can be accessed from the terminal at ~/Library/CloudStorage/SimDrop‑SimDrop/.

The utility works on macOS 15 or later and supports only iOS simulators, not physical devices. Dragging items moves them by default, mirroring iCloud Drive behavior; holding the Option key copies instead. SimDrop is free, open‑source under the GPL‑3.0 license, signed and notarized, and can be installed via Homebrew with brew install --cask rxliuli/tap/sim-drop. The author invited feedback and pull requests from users.
summary: SimDrop is a free, open‑source macOS utility that places each running iOS simulator in the Finder sidebar under Locations with Downloads and Photos & Videos folders. Simulators appear when they boot and disappear when shut down; the tool works on macOS 15+ and iOS simulators only and can be installed via Homebrew.
author: Hacker News

title: The Download: Better bionic hands and AI’s natural-gas boom
content:
The Download is a weekday newsletter that delivers a concise snapshot of the latest developments in technology. In this edition, two stories stand out: a breakthrough in prosthetic technology and a surge in natural‑gas usage driven by data‑center expansion.

The first story, written by Jessica Hamzelou, follows Avi Davidson, who lost his left hand as a teenager. After trying several prosthetic options, Davidson received a new generation of bionic hand that is wired directly to nerves in his forearm. The device now gives him the ability to feel pressure, enabling him to handle delicate objects such as grapes, eggs, or even a loved one’s hand. Davidson is the ninth person to receive the experimental implant, and he is the first to take it home and use it independently. Researchers hope that his experience will reveal how useful the technology is in everyday life and how it may affect his brain and nervous system.

The second piece, by Casey Crownhart, examines how data‑center growth is fueling a natural‑gas boom in the United States. In May 2025, David Rotman predicted that artificial intelligence would keep the country dependent on natural gas. Over the following eighteen months, that prediction has been repeatedly confirmed. A prime example is Meta’s data‑center plans in Louisiana, which have expanded from an initial three natural‑gas plants to ten. Meta’s emissions have risen 45 % over last year’s levels, and natural gas has become the default fuel for meeting the country’s rapidly increasing power demand. The article, sourced from The Spark, a weekly climate‑tech newsletter, outlines the implications of this trend for the future of the electrical grid.
summary: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: Costco offers $62.99 deal on Ocarina of Time Switch 2 cartridge
content:
The Nintendo Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has received a complete graphical overhaul and a range of quality‑of‑life updates that address issues from the original 1998 release, such as dungeon design and 3‑D navigation.  

For those still on their holiday wish‑lists, a few retailers are offering modest discounts. Costco members can buy the cartridge edition for $62.99, down from its regular price of $69.99, and this is the only retailer currently discounting the physical version. Both Amazon and Costco are selling the digital version for $54.99, a $5 reduction from the standard price of $59.99.  

The Switch 2 update also introduces a new gifting feature: players can designate up to eight members of a family group and send the digital game to them, where it appears gift‑wrapped on their home screen.  

The article concludes with a link to the full review of the remake.
summary: The Nintendo Switch 2 remake delivers a complete graphical overhaul and numerous quality-of-life updates to the ‘98 classic. | Image: Nintendo A lot of people have The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo Switch 2 on their holiday wishlist.
author: The Verge

title: GTA VI’s fictional Florida praised for lifelike transport, buildings and wildlife
content:
Grand Theft Auto VI has drawn fans in part because of its strong sense of place.  The game’s fictional rendition of Florida is described as the studio’s most lifelike setting yet, featuring functioning buses and trains, a variety of buildings that players can enter and explore, and residents they can chat with.  

The game also offers large outdoor areas where players can interact with wildlife, providing a contrast to the bright lights of the Miami‑like Vice City.  These elements combine with the long‑awaited release, relatable lead characters, a romantic storyline, and deep gameplay to explain the title’s popularity.
summary: GTA VI’s fictional rendition of Florida is described as the series’ most lifelike setting yet. It features functioning buses and trains, numerous interior buildings, chat‑able residents, and large wildlife areas outside the Miami‑like Vice City.
author: The Verge

title: Rockstar Games workers reject union vote, only 25% support
content:
Workers at Rockstar Games, the developer of Grand Theft Auto VI, rejected a union‑recognition vote that ran from November 12 to 26, coinciding with the game’s launch. Only 25 percent of employees voted in favor, so the formal recognition agreement failed.  

The Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB) said that Rockstar employees in the union will keep organizing despite the lack of formal status. If the vote had passed, it would have created a framework for collective bargaining over pay, overtime, bonuses, leave, pensions and a right to consultation on future changes, including the use of AI.
summary: Rockstar Games employees voted against a formal recognition agreement, with only 25 percent of votes in favor of unionization. The Independent Workers Union of Great Britain said organizing will continue despite the result, and the vote ran from November 12 through 26 during the GTA VI launch period.
author: The Verge
