title: Judge Loren AliKhan blocks FCC's early review of ABC broadcast licenses
content:
US District Judge Loren AliKhan issued a preliminary injunction that blocks the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from conducting an early review of ABC’s broadcast licenses.  The judge also rejected the FCC’s attempt to dismiss ABC’s First Amendment lawsuit.  

ABC has alleged that the FCC violated its free‑speech rights and that the agency “waged a retaliatory campaign” against the network over content it broadcast.  In her ruling, Judge AliKhan noted that the network is “likely to succeed on their retaliation claim.”  

Although Disney, ABC’s parent company, is not scheduled to renew its broadcast licenses until 2028, the FCC ordered the network to file for an ear last April.
summary: Judge Loren AliKhan blocks FCC's early review of ABC broadcast licenses.
author: The Verge

title: Google to require Android developers to publicly list phone number and address
content:
Google has announced that, starting next year, many independent Android app developers will be required to publish a phone number and address. The change is aimed at complying with European Union rules under the Digital Services Act, and Google says the contact details will be made public worldwide.  

Developers must decide by February 1, 2027 whether they qualify as a “trader” under UK and European law. Google defines a trader as someone who earns revenue from their apps, especially if the revenue is regular or high‑volume. Those who do not meet this definition will be exempt from the new disclosure requirement.
summary: Independent Android app developers are worried about their privacy after Google announced that from next year many of them will be required to share a phone number and address publicly. The policy change is intended to meet European Union regulations under the Digital Services Act, but Google says contact details will be made public worldwide.
author: The Verge

title: Garmin Forerunner 265S Drops to $300 for Black Friday
content:
The Garmin Forerunner 265S has dropped to $299.99, a $150 discount from its original MSRP of $449.99. The price cut is available at Amazon and Best Buy for Black Friday, making it the lowest price the watch has reached this year.  

The 265S is a 42 mm model that is identical to the standard 265 but offers a slightly longer battery life and a smaller build, making it a good fit for runners with petite wrists. Its OLED touchscreen contributes to the improved battery performance. The watch adds a splash of color and extra fitness‑tracking features while keeping the price lower than Garmin’s higher‑end models.  

Garmin’s platform is designed to receive firmware updates for several years after launch, allowing users to keep their devices current without needing the newest releases. This longevity means many Garmin users keep their watches for a long time, benefiting from continued software support.  

Other Garmin models on sale during Black Friday include the Fenix 8 at $749 (a 25 % discount), the Venu 4 at $449 (an 18 % discount), and the Forerunner 970 at $649 (a $100 discount). These options provide a range of features for outdoor sports, smartwatch‑style fitness tracking, and marathon‑ready performance.
summary: The Garmin Forerunner 265S, a slim 42mm fitness watch, is now available for $299.99 at Amazon and Best Buy during Black Friday. Its battery life is improved by its OLED touchscreen, making it a good choice for runners with smaller wrists.
author: The Verge

title: Midnight Diner quietly returns to Netflix
content:
Netflix’s expanding catalog now includes a growing library of reality shows, live‑programming, and even games, making it easier for viewers to overlook some of the platform’s best offerings. The author notes that this trend almost caused them to miss “Midnight Diner.”  

“Midnight Diner” is described as one of the most comforting shows available on Netflix. It follows the patrons of a cozy restaurant tucked away in the backstreets of Shinjuku, which remains open only during unusual hours. The series’ gentle premise and intimate setting have earned it a reputation for warmth and solace among viewers.
summary: Midnight Diner, a comforting Netflix series about patrons of a small Shinjuku restaurant, has returned to the platform. The show’s cozy atmosphere and late‑night setting made it easy to overlook amid Netflix’s expanding lineup.
author: The Verge

title: Study finds draining peatlands contributes a few percent of global warming
content:
Human‑caused climate change is often discussed in terms of fossil fuels, which are responsible for most of the problem. However, land‑use change also contributes significantly, accounting for about one‑third of total historical CO₂ emissions. While deforestation is a major factor, the removal of wetlands is another important source of greenhouse gases. Determining exactly how much the historical elimination of wetlands has added to warming has been difficult, but recent data on emissions from today’s surviving wetlands allow a clearer estimate.

A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—bogs and fens where organic matter builds up into thick layers. These peat stores hold roughly 600 billion tons of carbon, more than all of the world’s living vegetation combined. Because peatlands are permanently flooded, any oxygen in the water is quickly consumed, leaving anaerobic bacteria that decompose organic matter more slowly and incompletely.

In these anaerobic conditions, a portion of the organic carbon is converted into methane rather than CO₂. Methane is a far more potent greenhouse gas than CO₂, and it eventually oxidizes to CO₂. Thus, while most of the carbon in peatlands remains locked away, the carbon that does escape does so as methane, contributing disproportionately to warming.

The study’s findings, reflected in the headline that draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming, highlight the importance of protecting these carbon‑rich wetlands as part of climate mitigation efforts.
summary: Land‑use change accounts for about one‑third of historical CO₂ emissions, and a new MIT study led by Jevan Yu estimates that draining peatlands adds a few percent to global warming. Peatlands store roughly 600 billion tons of carbon, releasing some of it as methane when drained.
author: Ars Technica

title: Ford Unveils GT41 Hypercar in Bid to Win Le Mans Again
content: Sixty years ago, after two failed attempts, Ford won the 24 Hours of Le Mans with its GT40 race car. In the years since, the Blue Oval has been back to France more than a few times, with varying success. It could never replicate the GT40’s success winning overall, but it celebrated the 40th anniversary with a class win. Now it wants another shot at the really big trophy, and it debuted the car during the Detroit Lions-Chicago Bears football game today: meet the GT41. “Revealing the Ford GT41 is a significant moment for everyone involved in this program,” said Dan Sayers, manager of Ford Racing’s Hypercar program. “It's the result of an enormous amount of work across our engineering, design, and development teams and an important milestone on our journey towards 2027. We know the scale of the challenge ahead—the level of competition in Hypercar is incredibly high, and there are no shortcuts to success. Our focus has been on building the right foundations, bringing together the right people and making sure we learn as much as possible from every stage of development.” The video was directed by Zack Snyder and features Matt Damon’s voice-over. Like many other entrants in the World Endurance Championship’s Hypercar class, Ford has chosen the rear-wheel-drive LMDh technical approach rather than building the GT41 entirely from scratch, as Ferrari and Aston Martin do with their cars. LMDh cars start with one of four approved carbon fiber chassis—in this case, Ford is working with Oreca, which has also partnered with Genesis and Acura. Read full article Comments
summary: Ford Unveils GT41 Hypercar in Bid to Win Le Mans Again.
author: Ars Technica

title: Grand Theft Auto VI launch ranks among most successful entertainment releases
content:
The headline asserts that Grand Theft Auto VI demonstrates why efficiency is not a virtue.  

According to the report, the game—described as a “painstakingly human” video game—launched on the same day Anthropic entered the public market and became one of the most successful entertainment launches of all time.
summary: Grand Theft Auto VI became one of the most successful entertainment launches of all time. It achieved this on the same day Anthropic entered the public market, with the game described as a painstakingly human video game.
author: TechCrunch

title: X social network adds parental controls for teenagers after 20 years
content: Elon Musk’s social network X has introduced parental controls for teenagers. The new feature allows parents and guardians to manage the content their children can view on the platform. This marks the first time X offers such controls, announced after a 20‑year wait.
summary: Elon Musk's social network X has added parental controls for teenagers. The new tools let parents and guardians manage what their kids see on the platform.
author: TechCrunch

title: Unproven claim alleges former Megaspeed exec Alice Huang was a Chinese spy
content: The central, still‑unproven claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive, is a Chinese spy. Huang is alleged to have had an extramarital affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
summary: The central claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, is a Chinese spy. The allegation remains unproven and references her alleged extramarital affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
author: TechCrunch

title: Nvidia pauses server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia
content:
Nvidia has instructed its manufacturing partners to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia.  

The pause follows increased U.S. pressure aimed at preventing AI chips from reaching China.
summary: Nvidia has told manufacturing partners to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia as the U. S.
author: TechCrunch

title: Dressmaker review: charming PC business sim set in Twillford
content:
A new PC title from Cosy Lives and Free Lives, Dressmaker, places players in the role of a newly arrived dressmaker who runs the only clothing shop in the small town of Twillford. The town is abuzz after a local duke’s death, prompting ladies of standing to seek impressive funeral attire and other residents to request a range of garments, from respectful funeral frocks to bright‑coloured work outfits for farmers.

The game’s core loop involves talking to customers, gathering their style preferences and then drafting patterns in a sketchbook using fabric swatches and a pencil. Players can create a variety of designs, such as strapless bodices for elegant looks or pencil skirts for office wear. Reviewers describe Dressmaker as an absorbing, beautifully designed business simulation that delivers surprisingly thrilling challenges while catering to the exacting whims of the town’s inhabitants.
summary: Dressmaker is a PC business simulation game from Cosy Lives and Free Lives that puts players in the small town of Twillford as the only dressmaker. Players talk to customers, learn their style preferences and design outfits such as funeral frocks and farmer workwear using a sketchbook, fabric swatches and a pencil.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Tested 11 Wi‑Fi extenders and mesh systems to find fastest home network boost
content:
A recent review evaluated 11 Wi‑Fi range extenders and mesh networking systems to determine which deliver the fastest and most reliable connections for streaming, gaming and remote work. The testing aimed to identify devices that can overcome the limited coverage of typical broadband routers, which are often placed in hallways or corners and may not reach every room.

The article explains that Wi‑Fi extenders plug into a mains socket between the router and the desired location, rebroadcasting the signal to broaden coverage. Mesh systems, by contrast, use a primary router paired with one or two satellite units that cooperate to pass the connection from unit to unit, maintaining a strong link between devices and the internet throughout the home. Both solutions are presented as ways to improve connectivity when the existing router’s range is insufficient.
summary: We tested 11 range extenders and mesh systems to identify the fastest and most reliable options for streaming, gaming and working from home. Extenders plug into a mains socket to extend a router’s reach, while mesh systems pair a secondary router with one or two satellite units to provide continuous coverage throughout a home.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Hong Kong residents lay flowers for 168 Wang Fuk Court fire victims on anniversary
content: Hong Kong residents laid flowers and paid tribute to the 168 victims of the Wang Fuk Court fire in China, marking the first anniversary of the deadly disaster. The memorial reflects the community’s collective mourning one year after the tragedy.
summary: Hong Kong residents laid flowers and paid tribute to the 168 victims of the Wang Fuk Court fire in China. The ceremony marked one year after the deadly disaster.
author: Euronews

title: Argentina enters technical recession as weak consumption curtails Milei's gains
content: Argentina entered a technical recession after its economy contracted 1.8% in the third quarter, marking a second consecutive decline. The slowdown is attributed to weak consumer spending, reduced purchasing power and pressure on key sectors, factors that are diminishing the economic gains associated with President Javier Milei.
summary: Argentina's economy contracted 1.8% in the third quarter, marking a second consecutive decline. Weak consumption, falling purchasing power and strain in key sectors are slowing growth and clouding Javier Milei's prospects.
author: Euronews

title: NATO authorises AWACS deployment to Poland after missile incident
content: NATO has authorised the deployment of an AWACS reconnaissance aircraft to Poland following prosecutors’ report that three Russian cruise missiles landed on Polish territory. The airborne radar system, which has been in service since the Cold War, has previously operated in the Balkans, Libya and over U.S. airspace after the September 11 attacks.
summary: NATO has authorised deploying an AWACS reconnaissance aircraft to Poland after prosecutors said three Russian cruise missiles fell on its territory. The flying radar has served since the Cold War, in the Balkans, in Libya and over US airspace after 11 September.
author: Euronews

title: Kim Aris, Suu Kyi's son, relieved after first call in five years, questions military motives
content: In an interview on Euronews’ The World Conversation, Kim Aris said he felt “relieved” to hear his mother’s voice for the first time in five years. He urged stricter enforcement of sanctions and defended his mother’s record concerning the Rohingya genocide ruling.
summary: Kim Aris told Euronews’ The World Conversation that he felt relief hearing his mother Suu Kyi’s voice for the first time in five years. He urged tougher enforcement of sanctions, defended her record on the Rohingya genocide ruling, and questioned the military’s motives.
author: Euronews

title: 200 European farmers march in Brussels to protest EU CAP cuts
content: Around 200 representatives of European farming unions marched through Brussels on Thursday, 26 November 2026, driving tractors to protest proposed cuts to the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy. The demonstration took place as the European Union held a summit on its next long‑term budget.
summary: Around 200 representatives of European farming unions marched through Brussels, Belgium, on Thursday 26 November 2026 to protest proposed cuts to the European Union's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP). The demonstration coincided with a summit on the bloc's next long‑term budget.
author: Euronews

title: London's Gingerbread City returns with 50 edible architectural creations
content: London architects have revived the Gingerbread City exhibition, presenting 50 edible architectural creations that form a miniature city of gingerbread skyscrapers, sugar rivers and iconic landmarks. The festive display also incorporates commentary on the future of urban living.
summary: London architects have created a miniature city featuring gingerbread skyscrapers, sugar rivers and iconic landmarks. The festive exhibition also explores the future of urban living.
author: Euronews

title: Reporters Without Borders urges Arcom to suspend CNews for one month
content: Reporters Without Borders (RSF) urged France’s media regulator Arcom on Thursday to suspend the right‑wing television channel CNews for one month, citing the channel’s failure to uphold pluralism. CNews, owned by conservative billionaire Vincent Bolloré, responded by condemning the suspension request.
summary: Reporters Without Borders called on France's media regulator Arcom to suspend the right‑wing channel CNews for one month, saying it failed to uphold pluralism. The channel, owned by conservative billionaire Vincent Bolloré, condemned the call for its suspension.
author: France 24

title: Marine Le Pen condemns EU budget push ahead of French presidential election
content: EU leaders locked horns over the bloc's budget at a summit meeting in Brussels on Thursday, as far-right leader Marine Le Pen slammed an "underhanded" push to lock in the long-term spending plans before French presidential elections next year. European Council head Antonio Costa turned up the pressure upon arrival at the budget talks, where heavyweight Germany is pressing for cuts as well as burden-sharing on money for Ukraine. FRANCE 24's Dave Keating reports from Brussels.
summary: EU leaders clashed over the bloc's budget at a summit in Brussels on Thursday, with Marine Le Pen calling the effort to lock in long‑term spending plans before the French presidential election "underhanded". European Council head Antonio Costa arrived to increase pressure, while Germany urged cuts and greater burden‑sharing for Ukraine aid.
author: France 24

title: France's far-right leader Jordan Bardella accused of teenage anti‑Semitic comments
content:
French far‑right leader Jordan Bardella, 31, was confronted with new accusations on Thursday that he made anti‑Semitic remarks while a teenager. French media outlets released extracts from previously unaired conversations that were posted online, according to a report by FRANCE 24’s Solange Mougin.

Bardella, the top ally of Marine Le Pen, denied any wrongdoing. The allegations resurfaced after earlier claims in September that he had posted conspiracist comments about Jewish people on Facebook in 2013. The report does not provide further evidence or statements beyond Bardella’s denial.
summary: Jordan Bardella, a 31‑year‑old French far‑right leader and top ally of Marine Le Pen, faced new accusations on Thursday of making anti‑Semitic remarks as a teenager after media released extracts of unaired conversations. He denied any wrongdoing regarding the alleged 2013 Facebook comments.
author: France 24

title: Trump Urges Putin to Pull Back Military Aggression in Europe
content:
Donald Trump said on Thursday that he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to “pull back all military aggression” against Europe. Trump noted that he had called Putin his friend only a week earlier and that he made the request during their meeting in China last week, adding that he believed it could help lead to a deal to end Moscow’s war in Ukraine.

The comments came a day after Trump hosted NATO chief Mark Rutte in Florida, where the two issued a joint statement urging Russia not to expand the Ukraine war. The statement was explained by FRANCE 24’s international affairs editor Kethevane Gorjestani.
summary: US President Donald Trump asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to pull back all military aggression against Europe during a meeting in China. The request followed a joint statement with NATO chief Mark Rutte calling on Russia not to expand the Ukraine war.
author: France 24

title: Hamas considers response after Israel kills 10 Palestinians in Gaza
content:
Five Israeli strikes and a shooting overnight and on Thursday killed 10 Palestinians across Gaza, officials at Shifa and Al‑Aqsa Martyrs hospitals said. One of the strikes hit a residential apartment in Deir Al‑Balah in central Gaza, killing a man and his wife.

The deaths have prompted Hamas to weigh a response, according to the article’s headline. FRANCE 24’s Jennie Shin interviewed journalist Ahmed Dremly, who was in Gaza until six months ago and has extensively covered the humanitarian crisis there.
summary: Five Israeli strikes and a shooting overnight and on Thursday killed 10 Palestinians across Gaza, according to officials at Shifa and Al‑Aqsa Martyrs hospitals. A strike on a residential apartment in Deir Al‑Balah in central Gaza killed a man and his wife, the officials said.
author: France 24

title: Spain's PM Pedro Sanchez calls snap election amid coalition housing rift
content:
Pedro Sánchez has spent eight years as a prominent figure among European leaders, known for snatching victories from the jaws of defeat. Yet questions arise whether he has run out of options this time.

The Socialist prime minister faces accusations of incumbent fatigue and nepotism. Sánchez has gambled on turning a coalition rift over Spain’s housing shortage into a referendum on the country’s strong growth, and he has called a snap general election.
summary: Spain's Socialist prime minister Pedro Sanchez is facing incumbent fatigue and nepotism allegations. He turned a coalition dispute over the housing shortage into a referendum on strong growth by calling a snap general election.
author: France 24

title: Iranian monarchist supporters disrupt Paris women's rights event attended by French FM
content: A Paris event on Iranian women’s rights, attended by French Foreign Minister Jean‑Noël Barrot, was disrupted by diaspora supporters of Reza Pahlavi, the US‑based son of Iran’s deposed shah. The supporters taunted left‑leaning opponents of Iran’s Islamic regime, underscoring the deep divisions in the Iranian diaspora as the Iran war enters its tenth month.
summary: A Paris event on Iranian women's rights attended by French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot was disrupted by diaspora supporters of Reza Pahlavi. The supporters taunted left‑leaning opponents of Iran's Islamic regime, highlighting bitter divides in the Iranian diaspora as the Iran war enters its tenth month.
author: France 24

title: EU-Indonesia trade deal opens new markets but poses challenges
content: The EU‑Indonesia trade agreement creates fresh export and investment prospects for both Jakarta and Brussels. However, it remains uncertain whether Indonesia can convert Europe’s increasing interest in its markets and critical minerals into sustainable domestic gains.
summary: The agreement offers new export and investment opportunities for Jakarta and Brussels. Indonesia must determine how to turn Europe's growing interest in its markets and critical minerals into sustainable gains.
author: DW World

title: FIFA says cyberattack targeted limited personal and business data
content: FIFA announced that a recent cyberattack was directed at a limited set of personal and business information. The organization noted that the breach occurred during a sensitive period for the governing body and its president, Gianni Infantino.
summary: FIFA said a cyberattack targeted personal and business information. The attack occurred at a sensitive time for the organization and its president Gianni Infantino.
author: DW World

title: African opposition says arrests and restrictions hinder challenges to power
content: Opposition politicians and government critics across Africa report that arrests, prosecutions and limits on public activity are increasingly hindering their ability to challenge those in power, suggesting a possible broader pattern of pressure on dissenting voices.
summary: Opposition politicians and government critics say arrests, prosecutions and restrictions on public activity are making it harder to challenge those in power. They question whether a broader pattern of pressure is emerging.
author: DW World

title: Thousands protest in Kurdish region capital over Baghdad plan to control oil and borders
content: Thousands gathered in the capital of Iraq’s semi‑autonomous Kurdish region, waving flags and protesting plans for the federal government in Baghdad to assume control of oil operations and border crossings. Demonstrators voiced opposition to the proposed takeover.
summary: Thousands gathered in the capital of northern Iraq's semiautonomous Kurdish region, waving flags. They voiced opposition to plans by the federal government to take control of oil operations and border crossings.
author: DW World

title: Saudi pop music expands under Vision 2030 with state funding, musicians optimistic
content: Saudi Arabia’s music scene has expanded dramatically under Vision 2030, with state funding and support driving the growth. Local musicians and DJs say they feel optimistic about the changes. Observers note a question remains whether this cultural boost is inadvertently supporting an authoritarian government.
summary: Saudi Arabia's music scene has evolved hugely thanks to state funding and support as part of Vision 2030. Local musicians and DJs are optimistic, though some wonder if they are helping prop up an authoritarian state.
author: DW World

title: Albanian youth protest in Flamingo Revolution, say fewer plan to emigrate
content: Youth protests dubbed the “Flamingo Revolution” in Albania are targeting what demonstrators describe as a rigid political system and corruption, and have shaken the government of Prime Minister Edi Rama. The demonstrations also suggest that fewer young Albanians are now choosing to emigrate in search of a better future.
summary: Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. The protests also indicate that fewer young Albanians are willing to emigrate for a better future.
author: DW World

title: UN peacekeepers increase civilian protection in Ebola‑hit Ituri after Djugu clashes
content: United Nations peacekeepers in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have increased civilian‑protection activities in Ebola‑affected Ituri province after renewed armed clashes erupted in Djugu territory. The stepped‑up efforts aim to safeguard residents amid the ongoing fighting.
summary: United Nations peacekeepers in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have stepped up efforts to protect civilians in Ebola‑hit Ituri province. The increase follows renewed armed clashes in Djugu territory.
author: UN News

title: Maritime trade stagnates as seaborne shipments slow, hitting poorest nations
content: UN economists said on Thursday that seaborne trade, a key driver of the global economy, continues to slow. They noted that conflict‑related and climate‑related disruptions are affecting least‑developed economies and small island nations most severely, underscoring a broader stagnation in maritime trade amid geopolitical uncertainty.
summary: UN economists said on Thursday that seaborne trade that underpins the global economy continues to slow. They said disruption from conflict and climate-related factors is hitting least-developed economies and small island nations hardest.
author: UN News

title: Russia readies nuclear‑armed Sputnik‑S satellite for launch within 60 days
content: Russia has assembled a satellite known as Sputnik‑S that is equipped to carry a nuclear device. German media, referencing western intelligence assessments, report that the satellite could be launched within 60 days and become operational shortly thereafter, with a launch planned for later this year. Officials say the presence of a nuclear‑armed satellite in orbit could represent a significant threat to global communications. No further details about the satellite’s capabilities or intended use were provided.
summary: Sputnik‑S, a nuclear‑enabled satellite assembled by Russia, could be launched within 60 days, reports say. German media citing western intelligence assessments say the satellite could become operational shortly after launch and could pose a significant threat to global communications.
author: Guardian World

title: UK net migration falls to lowest level since 1997, Labour credits policies
content: Labour is jubilant it has got numbers down to levels the Tories could not but it was helped by factors beyond its control Net migration to UK falls to lowest level since 1997 excluding pandemic David Cameron was the leader of the opposition when he made a comment on overall migration that was used to interrogate every Tory leader for the next 14 years. Asked in January 2010 on the BBC by the interviewer Andrew Marr to address comments made by the archbishop of Canterbury calling for the population to remain under 70 million, Cameron said net immigration levels of 200,000 a year were “too much”.
summary: UK net migration falls to lowest level since 1997, Labour credits policies.
author: Guardian World

title: AEC to review $1m One Nation donations from Gina Rinehart allies Adam Giles, Ian Plimer
content:
The Australian Electoral Commission will review $1 million in donations to the One Nation party that were made by Adam Giles and Ian Plimer, identified as close associates of the party’s billionaire benefactor Gina Rinehart. The two contributions each total $500,000 and were given to the Pauline Hanson‑led party.

Special Minister of State Don Farrell said on Thursday that the information on these donations could lead to further regulatory action if the gifts are found to breach provisions of the Electoral Act.
summary: The Australian Electoral Commission will review two $500,000 donations to the Pauline Hanson‑led One Nation party made by Adam Giles and Ian Plimer, close associates of billionaire Gina Rinehart. Special minister of state Don Farrell said the donations could face further regulatory action if they breach the Electoral Act.
author: Guardian World

title: Beau Lamarre-Condon convicted of murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies with police weapon
content:
Video released of Beau Lamarre‑Condon shows the officer in 2020 deploying a Taser at close range to an Indigenous man’s face, chest and neck. The footage was cited after Lamarre‑Condon, who was serving as a New South Wales police officer, was found to have been under review by the force for repeatedly using his Taser on that man four years before the murders.

On 19 February 2024 Lamarre‑Condon killed Jesse Baird and Luke Davies with his police service weapon. A 12‑person jury convicted him on Wednesday of both murders. The case notes his prior disciplinary review but provides no further detail on recruitment processes.
summary: Beau Lamarre-Condon, a serving New South Wales police officer, killed Jesse Baird and Luke Davies with his service weapon on 19 February 2024. He had been under review for repeatedly using his Taser on a man in 2020, and a 12‑person jury convicted him on Wednesday.
author: Guardian World

title: Sydney fire ant outbreak blamed on ignored biosecurity recommendations
content: Farmers’ Federation president says Australia ‘can’t even keep [illicit] cigarettes out of the country … let alone some of these difficult-to-detect pests’ Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast Years-old recommendations by Australia’s biosecurity watchdog have been ignored or not acted on by successive federal governments, increasing the risk of an invasive pest outbreak such as the fire ants discovered in Sydney this week, according to experts. Environmentalists and biosecurity experts warn the large colony of red imported fire ants are a warning sign that the country’s quarantine system is too slow-moving, underfunded and overly concerned with agriculture.
summary: Sydney fire ant outbreak blamed on ignored biosecurity recommendations.
author: Guardian World

title: Coalition and Labor approve 20% gas reservation scheme for major exporters
content:
Coalition members voted in the Senate to approve a federal gas reservation scheme, the government’s final major piece of legislation for 2026. The scheme requires Australia’s largest exporters to set aside up to 20 % of their product for domestic use.

In a late sitting on Thursday night, opposition senators voted with the government, giving Labor the numbers needed to pass the measure.

The vote also denied the Greens’ proposal for a 25 % tax on exports.
summary: The Coalition and Labor voted together in the Senate on Thursday night to approve a federal gas reservation scheme that requires Australia’s largest exporters to keep up to 20% of their product for domestic use. The vote also denied the Greens’ bid for a 25% export tax, delivering the government’s final major legislation for 2026.
author: Guardian World

title: Southern and central Australia face heightened bushfire risk and heatwaves this summer
content:
Fire chiefs warn that large swathes of southern and central Australia are facing an elevated bushfire risk this summer. The seasonal outlook released on Friday by the Australian and New Zealand Council for Fire and Emergency Services (AFAC) cites high fuel loads, low soil moisture and forecast hot, dry conditions as the drivers of the threat.

According to the AFAC report, most of Victoria, eastern Tasmania and extensive areas of South Australia, Western Australia, New South Wales and the Northern Territory are at heightened risk. Nationwide, heatwaves and extreme temperatures are also expected.
summary: Southern and central Australia face heightened bushfire risk and heatwaves this summer.
author: Guardian World

title: Lana Nusseibeh in UK to promote UN secretary‑general bid, downplay UAE diplomat past
content:
Lana Nusseibeh, the candidate backed by the United States and Russia for United Nations secretary‑general, is in Britain this week on a “charm offensive.” She is meeting ministers, MPs and academics and will take part in a public event with the UN Association as she seeks to present herself as a potential future secretary‑general.  

Nusseibeh is also trying to shift attention from her former role as a United Arab Emirates diplomat who denied the UAE’s involvement in arming a militia accused of war crimes and genocide in Sudan’s four‑year civil war, and to overcome reported resistance in London to her bid.
summary: The US and Russia’s candidate for secretary general is on a charm offensive. Can she overcome London’s resistance to her bid?

title: ISS Astronauts Celebrate Thanksgiving with Space‑Grown Plants and Hot Sauce
content:
NASA astronaut Anil Menon detailed his plans for a nontraditional Thanksgiving meal aboard the International Space Station in a video released on Monday, Nov. 23. In the 2.5-minute clip, Menon, who was wearing a chef’s toque, discussed the importance of growing plants in orbit to support future missions to the moon and Mars. He stated that the crew must grow their own nutrition for these future endeavors. For his specific meal, Menon said he intends to combine the space-grown plants with a tortilla, pasta, and hot sauce. He also expressed gratitude to his family and the people watching the video.

Fellow crew members joined Menon to share their own holiday plans and sentiments. NASA astronaut Luke Delaney did not discuss food but instead expressed gratitude for his family, crewmates, and support network on Earth. NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins provided an overview of the broader Thanksgiving menu available in space, listing roasted turkey, mac and cheese, mashed potatoes, and candied yams. She displayed small bags containing these items, noting that the crew should be in good shape for the holiday.

Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut Joshua Kutryk stated that he would eat rice and the space-grown plants raw, explaining that consuming the plants raw reminds him of Earth, which he misses. Following their individual statements, all four astronauts wished viewers a happy Thanksgiving and performed zero-gravity flips and rolls, causing the space plants to move around the cabin.

The four astronauts featured in the video are part of the current crew on the International Space Station. Delaney, Kutryk, and Watkins are members of SpaceX’s Crew-13 mission, which arrived at the station on Oct. 1. A fourth Crew-13 member, Sergey Teteryatnikov of the Russian space agency Roscosmos, is also on board. They share the station with Menon and cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina, who arrived in July aboard a Russian Soyuz spacecraft.

Celebrating major holidays together on the ISS is a tradition that reinforces the strong bonds between crewmates and helps them cope with being away from friends and family. The CSA recently announced that Kutryk’s wife gave birth to the couple’s third child, a daughter. In a statement shared by the CSA, the couple said they feel incredibly connected despite the distance and are looking forward to reuniting their family of five.
summary: NASA astronaut Anil Menon showed the space‑grown plants he will use with tortilla, pasta and hot sauce for Thanksgiving. The crew also shared a menu that includes roasted turkey, mac and cheese, mashed potatoes, candied yams, rice and raw space‑grown plants, wishing viewers a happy holiday.
author: Space.com

title: Julie Delpy Discusses Writing Six Screenplays and Long Work Hours
content: Thirty years after the roles that made her famous, the star of Three Colours: White and the Before trilogy is busier than ever – as a screenwriter and director. But, she says, a lot of people have tried to keep her down To listen to Julie Delpy talk about her workload is to feel the need for a nap coming on. She is writing six screenplays at the moment that range from dark comedies to thrillers. “I don’t do monoculture,” she says. If her producer hadn’t reined her in, she would be working on five horror film scripts too. The actor, writer and director says she doesn’t sleep well – she can sit at her desk for up to 18 hours, writing “until I run out of steam. I know you could think I’m exaggerating. I’m not. If you look at my computer, you will see how bad it is.” We’re on a video call, Delpy from her home in Los Angeles. She is charming – intense and funny in big black-framed glasses. “I look so weird with this angle on my hair,” she says, of the ceiling light behind her. “Like an angry bald man!”
summary: Julie Delpy is writing six screenplays ranging from dark comedies to thrillers, and would add five horror scripts if not for her producer's constraints. She works up to 18 hours at a desk and often struggles to sleep.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Aaron Rodgers' exit from Pittsburgh Steelers signals potential franchise collapse
content:
The departure of quarterback Aaron Rodgers from the Pittsburgh Steelers has concluded a relationship described as a “marriage of convenience” that ended in “spectacular flames.” The article suggests that this messy exit may signal an overdue collapse for the franchise, which has been characterized as one of the NFL’s most chaotic soap operas for the past decade. The author notes that, aside from owner Art Rooney II, few were surprised by the outcome, particularly after the Steelers hired a coach with whom Rodgers had previously fallen out in Green Bay.

Tensions between Rodgers and the coaching staff had been evident during the first eleven weeks of the season. The text highlights a specific incident in early October where Rodgers yelled, “What the fuck … call it!” at coach McCarthy while searching for a play. This interaction served as a hint of the approaching drama, reinforcing the view that the team’s internal conflicts were inevitable given the prior history between the quarterback and the coaching staff.
summary: Aaron Rodgers' exit from the Pittsburgh Steelers has raised concerns about a potential collapse of the franchise. Rodgers publicly criticized the team's situation, yelling at coach McCarthy and referencing past conflicts with a former Green Bay coach.
author: Guardian Sport

title: David Warner Demands Credible Evidence for New Superglue and Grit Ball Tampering Claims
content: Former Test opener accuses media of perpetuating speculation Warner calls out ‘unverified claims’ about Australian ball tampering David Warner has accused the media of “perpetuating speculation” as the sandpaper scandal continues to simmer. The former Australia batter has called for media to substantiate allegations that he used superglue and grit on finger strapping to tamper with the ball on the infamous 2018 tour of South Africa. The claims, published by News Corp and SEN radio, were penned by prominent broadcaster Gerard Whateley.
summary: Former Test opener David Warner accuses the media of perpetuating speculation about his alleged use of superglue and grit on finger strapping to tamper with the ball during the 2018 South Africa tour. The claims were published by News Corp and SEN radio and written by broadcaster Gerard Whateley.
author: Guardian Sport

title: ‘Not Bayern-like’: Joshua Kimmich fumes at club’s treatment of Jamal Musiala
content:
Bundesliga champions Bayern Munich fell 2‑1 to Lille on Wednesday, a defeat that prompted midfielder Joshua Kimmich to launch a sharp criticism of the club’s handling of teammate Jamal Musiala. Kimmich, the club’s vice‑captain, described the treatment as “not Bayern‑like” and defended Musiala’s neurological condition that causes seizures.

Musiala’s condition has led to repeated seizures, including two on the field during pre‑season games. Senior Bayern figures have publicly questioned his performances and contract, a stance that drew protests from the players’ union Fifpro. Kimmich warned that Bayern risked undermining its family image if it continued to treat Musiala in this manner.
summary: ‘Not Bayern-like’: Joshua Kimmich fumes at club’s treatment of Jamal Musiala.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Damallsvenskan Declines from Summit of Women’s Football in Sweden
content:
The Damallsvenskan once dominated European women’s football, drawing the continent’s top players. Today, however, many stakeholders express concern about the league’s future viability.  

On 12 October 2003, Sweden’s national team faced Germany in the World Cup final. TV4 broke its own record as almost half of the nation tuned in. The match went into extra time, and Nia Künzer scored the golden goal at 98 minutes, ending the game in Sweden’s favour.  

Despite the bitter loss, observers believed the high‑profile match would spark a commercial breakthrough for women’s football in Sweden, making it difficult for sponsors and broadcasters to ignore the sport’s growing interest.
summary: Damallsvenskan once mastered Europe and attracted the best players but many are now worried for its future. In 2003, Sweden's women's national team played Germany in the World Cup final, drawing a record TV4 audience as almost half the nation watched, and Nia Künzer scored the golden goal after 98 minutes.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Nations Championship plans relegation playoffs risk unions’ ire
content:
From 2030, the Nations Championship may introduce relegation, allowing two bottom teams to drop out of the competition.  

The proposed mechanism is a one‑legged playoff between the bottom sides in both the northern and southern tables and the winners of the equivalent tables in the tier‑two Nations Cup, which is run by World Rugby. The Guardian learned of these plans; tier‑one teams are expected to push back.
summary: The Nations Championship organisers plan to introduce relegation playoffs starting in 2030, which could see two teams relegated. Bottom sides in both northern and southern hemisphere tables would play one-legged matches against the winners of the equivalent tables in the tier two Nations Cup run by World Rugby.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Pochettino claims officials ‘punished’ Manchester United in chaotic Sporting draw
content:
Mauricio Pochettino has said that Manchester United were “punished” after a chaotic 2‑2 draw with Sporting, citing faulty officiating that he believes unfairly affected the match. He questioned the “difficult to understand” decisions made by the referee and noted that Zirkzee has joined him in offering support to Lammens.

The referee, Szymon Marciniak, ruled Amad Diallo’s first‑half strike off after deciding that Youri Tielemans had fouled Gonçalo Inácio. Tielemans was booked, and when he received a second yellow in added time he was sent off, giving United their fifth red card in the last nine games. This incident followed Leny Yoro’s red card in Sunday’s 4‑0 loss at Liverpool, which was later rescinded.
summary: Pochettino claims officials ‘punished’ Manchester United in chaotic Sporting draw.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Gary Neville and Michael Carrick film intro at Manchester podcast studio
content:
In a Manchester podcast studio, a production runner can be seen pouring water into jugs as Gary Neville and former player Michael Carrick enter the set. Neville explains that filming is already underway and that the opening segment is designed to show everyone arriving and engaging in light banter. He says this “humanises us” and makes viewers think they are simply mates chatting about football, rather than members of a global podcast empire that feels compelled to churn out endless provocative content for profit.

The piece highlights how even the best managers find it difficult to escape the ex‑players’ tendency to manufacture a crisis for material. The author notes that Neville’s approach attempts to balance authenticity with the commercial demands of the medium, asking rhetorically, “why can’t you be both?”
summary: In a Manchester podcast studio, Gary Neville entered with Michael Carrick while a production runner poured water into jugs. Neville said the intro segment was intended to humanise them as mates chatting about football rather than a commercial podcast empire.

content:
New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill (D) declared a state of emergency on Wednesday as a nor’easter moved up the East Coast. The storm brought heavy rain, high winds, and delayed thousands of flights.

Sherrill warned that damaging winds, heavy rain, and severe tidal flooding are expected through Friday, with the most dangerous conditions on Thanksgiving Day.
summary: New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency on Wednesday as a nor’easter moved up the East Coast, bringing heavy rain, high winds, and delaying thousands of flights. content: The U.S. Army detonated a degraded stockpile of lead‑based munitions at its Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, early Wednesday. The controlled explosion proceeded despite earlier public‑health concerns that had delayed the plan. Army officials said the detonation was necessary to prevent an unintended explosion.

content: A federal judge ruled against the Democratic National Committee in a lawsuit concerning taxpayer-funded pro-President Trump advertisements aired earlier this year. The DNC had contended that the ads would influence the outcome of the November midterm election. According to new court filings, the judge had previously issued a temporary restraining order related to the case.

content: New York Governor Kathy Hochul (D) declared a state of emergency on Wednesday for New York City, Nassau, Suffolk, and Westchester counties as a powerful Thanksgiving storm approaches. The declaration comes after the storm has already disrupted travel in the region.

D.) over the House‑passed Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent. Scott has pledged to secure a vote on the bill before Christmas, citing strong support from Trump.

title: Court allows Puerto Rico governor to fire LUMA Energy, nullifying its grid contract
content: A court decision permits Puerto Rico’s governor to terminate LUMA Energy, the firm that has run the island’s electric grid for five years. The ruling nullifies LUMA’s contract and gives the government one year to find a new operator for the power system.
summary: LUMA Energy took over Puerto Rico's electric grid five years ago. A court ruling nullifies LUMA's contract and gives the government one year to find a new operator.

title: The dhow builders crafting giant historic ships in India – in pictures
content:
In Mandvi, a 16th-century port city on India’s west coast founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, shipbuilders spend three years completing commissions for traditional dhows. The city’s strategic location along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, where it flows into the Arabian Sea, allowed it to become a dynamic hub in western Indian Ocean maritime networks. Historically, Mandvi prospered by exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals, and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses, and luxury goods.

The construction process is described as both cultural and technical. In local shipyards, a stemson, a piece of supporting timber in the bow of a boat, is carved from teak. This work is performed under the supervision of the master shipwright, known as a mistri, who designs boats without written plans. The accompanying visual documentation of these giant historic ships was captured by photographer Frédéric Noy.
summary: The dhow builders crafting giant historic ships in India – in pictures.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Lawsuit claims Louisiana land deal between SpaceX and ExxonMobil breached open meetings law
content:
A new lawsuit filed by three residents of south-central Louisiana alleges that state and Vermilion Parish officials violated the state’s open meetings law while approving a land deal between SpaceX and ExxonMobil. The suit claims that the parish board was manipulated to allow the transaction to proceed and that a related settlement agreement was hidden from the public.

The dispute concerns 125,000 acres of marshland formerly owned by ExxonMobil, which SpaceX is set to access following the conclusion of a previous lawsuit regarding wetlands damage. According to the filing, officials violated open meetings laws eight times during the facilitation of this agreement. The plaintiffs assert these actions were intended to keep the public uninformed about the measures being taken for SpaceX.

This legal challenge follows the recent approval of a tax incentive package for SpaceX’s Starbase Louisiana project, which officials announced over the summer. The lawsuit characterizes the $27.5 billion incentive package as a record-breaking deal.
summary: A lawsuit filed by three residents claims that Vermilion Parish officials manipulated a board to approve a 125,000‑acre land deal between SpaceX and ExxonMobil, hiding the settlement from the public. The suit alleges the officials violated Louisiana’s open meetings law eight times while approving a record $27.5 bn tax‑incentive package for SpaceX’s Starbase Louisiana project.

title: Gut microbiome may shape blood sugar benefits of whole grains
content: People with prediabetes face a very high risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Improving their diet is identified as one method they can use to try to prevent the progression of the disease.
summary: People with prediabetes are at very high risk for developing type 2 diabetes. Improving their diet is one way they can try to fend off advanced disease.

title: Fathers' Antidepressant Use Before Pregnancy Raises Children's Blood Pressure Risk
content: A large Danish study published in The BMJ reports that paternal antidepressant use in the months preceding pregnancy is associated with a slightly increased risk of metabolic disorders in offspring. The research specifically identifies a link to higher rates of high blood pressure in the children.
summary: A large Danish study published in The BMJ found that fathers who used antidepressants in the months before pregnancy had a slightly increased risk of metabolic disorders in their children. The study highlighted high blood pressure as the most common disorder linked to the fathers' antidepressant use.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Ebola outbreak in Congo tops 12,000 cases amid fighting
content: The fast‑moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday. Fighting between rebels and the army disrupts containment efforts, and violence has forced some responders to evacuate.
summary: The outbreak in eastern Congo has exceeded 12,000 confirmed cases, according to government data. Fighting between rebels and the army has disrupted containment efforts and forced some responders to evacuate.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Gene that Sets Neuron Identity Also Controls Synaptic Inputs, Study Finds
content: A new study by neuroscientists at King’s College London shows that a gene involved in determining a neuron’s identity also influences the number of synaptic inputs that neuron receives. The research, performed in the developing mouse brain, found that the molecules neurons use to connect depend on the future role the neuron will play in the adult brain. It also revealed that the patterns of connections formed are shaped by the electrical activity of the neurons during development.
summary: A gene that defines neuron identity also influences the number of synaptic inputs a neuron receives. Researchers at King's College London found that the molecules used to wire neurons in the developing mouse brain depend on the neurons' future roles and on their electrical activity during development.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Low disease flare risk for IBD patients using assisted reproductive technology
content: A recent study published online on Nov. 10 in Inflammatory Bowel Diseases reports that women with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) who undergo assisted reproductive technology (ART) experience low rates of disease flare. The research also found that their live‑birth rates are comparable to those of the general population.
summary: A study published online Nov. 10 in Inflammatory Bowel Diseases found that patients with inflammatory bowel disease undergoing assisted reproductive technology have low flare rates. The study also reported that live birth rates are comparable to those of the general population.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Osaka Metropolitan University researchers strengthen protein to better hold anticancer drug
content: Researchers at Osaka Metropolitan University have altered a naturally occurring protein to increase its binding strength to an anticancer drug. The modification aims to keep the drug from being released prematurely, ensuring it reaches its intended target before release.
summary: Researchers from Osaka Metropolitan University modified a naturally occurring protein to hold an anticancer drug more tightly. The modification may prevent the drug from being released before it reaches its intended destination.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Lynne Balmain cites NHS wait for ADHD assessment as financial and mental health strain
content:
The article highlights the challenges of obtaining an ADHD or autism diagnosis through the NHS, noting that long waiting times can create significant obstacles for patients.

Lynne Balmain reports that the delay in receiving an ADHD assessment not only imposes financial pressure but also negatively affects her mental health and overall wellbeing.
summary: Lynne Balmain says the wait for an ADHD assessment causes not just financial pressure. She says it also impacts her mental health and wellbeing.
author: BBC Health

title: Judge blocks Brendan Carr-led FCC from taking any further action against ABC’s licenses
content:
A federal judge, Loren L AliKhan, granted a preliminary injunction on Wednesday that blocks the Brendan Carr‑led Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from taking any action that would restrict ABC’s ability to renew its broadcast licenses. The injunction follows ABC’s August lawsuit against the FCC over an unusual demand that the network apply early to renew eight local licenses for stations it owns.

The FCC said the early‑renewal process was needed to obtain documents related to an ongoing Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) investigation. ABC countered that the demand was a punishment for editorial coverage it said was critical of the Trump administration. The FCC’s order came after Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump criticized ABC for a comment made by late‑night host Jimmy Kimmel.
summary: Judge blocks Brendan Carr-led FCC from taking any further action against ABC’s licenses.
author: Guardian Business

title: Australia talks with ESA to fly director Katherine Bennell-Pegg as first funded astronaut
content: Australia is in talks with the European Space Agency (ESA) about sending Katherine Bennell‑Pegg to space. Bennell‑Pegg, director of space technology at the Australian Space Agency, completed ESA training in 2024 and would become the first officially funded Australian astronaut if accepted.
summary: Australia is in talks with the European Space Agency about potentially sending Katherine Bennell-Pegg on a future space mission. Bennell-Pegg, the director of space technology at the Australian Space Agency who completed ESA training in 2024, would become the first officially funded Australian astronaut if selected.
author: Phys.org

title: Peregrine falcon habitat in UK could grow 74% by 2080 due to climate change
content: A new study indicates that global warming could make the United Kingdom a more hospitable environment for the world’s fastest bird, the peregrine falcon. The research projects that suitable habitat for the species could expand by 74 % by 2080 under a high‑emissions climate scenario.
summary: A new study indicates that the area suitable for peregrine falcons within the UK could expand by 74% by 2080. This potential growth in livable territory is projected to occur under a high-emissions climate scenario.
author: Phys.org

title: Dragonflies Feast on Insects and Each Other During Autumn Migrations
content: New research indicates that dragonflies consume a variety of insects, including one another, during their autumn migrations. Scientists conducted this study at the Pass of Bujaruelo in the Pyrenees, a 30-meter gap between two high peaks that serves as a migration route for millions of insects annually.
summary: Dragonflies feast on a host of insects—and each other—during their autumn migrations, new research shows. Scientists studied dragonflies at the Pass of Bujaruelo—a 30-meter (98-foot) gap between two high peaks in the Pyrenees, through which millions of insects migrate every year.
author: Phys.org

title: FCC Approves SpaceX's Plan to Deploy 1 Million Satellites for Space Data Centers
content: The Trump administration authorized SpaceX to deploy one million satellites intended to establish data centers in space, fulfilling a long-standing objective for Elon Musk’s company. This regulatory approval has prompted skepticism and alarm among certain scientists regarding the proposed orbital infrastructure.
summary: The Trump administration approved SpaceX's plan to deploy 1 million satellites to create data centers in space. The decision has sparked skepticism and alarm among some scientists.
author: Phys.org

title: Miniature Cas12m proteins shown to cleave DNA
content: An international research team led by graduate student Hayato Morinaga, Assistant Professor Satoshi N. Omura, and Professor Osamu Nureki of the University of Tokyo has shown that certain miniature Cas12m proteins possess an active state capable of cleaving DNA. The group also mapped the structural differences between the active and inactive variants.
summary: An international research group led by graduate student Hayato Morinaga, Assistant Professor Satoshi N. Omura and Professor Osamu Nureki from the University of Tokyo demonstrated that some Cas12m proteins have an active state that can cleave DNA. The team also clarified the structural differences between the active and inactive variations.
author: Phys.org

title: King tide waves batter California coast, soak San Francisco, trigger evacuations
content:
Massive waves carried on king tides battered California coast Wednesday, prompting evacuations.  

The waves soaked San Francisco, but spared feared mass disruptions to Thanksgiving holiday travel.
summary: Massive king tide waves battered California's coast on Wednesday, prompting evacuations and soaking San Francisco. The storms did not cause the feared mass disruptions to Thanksgiving holiday travel.
author: Phys.org

title: Associate professor Jonté Myers highlights need for math fact fluency interventions
content: Associate professor Jonté Myers notes that fluency with mathematics facts is essential for overall mathematics proficiency, yet many students encounter difficulty in acquiring these foundational skills. The focus is on interventions aimed at improving fact fluency for learners who experience mathematics difficulties.
summary: Associate professor Jonté Myers says developing fluency with mathematics facts is key to mathematics proficiency. He notes that many students struggle to develop these foundational skills.
author: Phys.org

title: AI Solves Riemann Hypothesis and Navier-Stokes, Raising Questions About Limits
content: Alzheimer’s disease, involving amyloid plaques in the brain, will be tough for AI to solve JUAN GAERTNER/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY The progress AI has made in mathematics this year is nothing short of extraordinary. In January, I was impressed to see relatively minor open problems tackled with the help of AI. Now, AI is being used to solve the hardest problems in maths. The obvious next question is, if AI can do this, is there anything it can’t do? That is the inference that the AI companies want us to make, but, in reality, the answer is much more nuanced. Mathematicians are amazed by ‘holy grail’ proof of Riemann hypothesis We see this messaging in claims that AI can “solve X”, where X is any field of human endeavour you care to name. Biology is a big one. “Cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, mental illness – these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade,” said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei while promoting the company’s recent initial public offering. “I think one day maybe we can cure all disease with the help of AI,” said Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind, last year, adding that this could be “within the next decade or so”. This phenomenon isn’t new: I call it “physicist brain”, after the propensity for physicists to wade into areas outside their expertise and declare simple solutions. More broadly, it is called Nobel disease, after the many Nobel prizewinners who have gone on to make, shall we say, less evidenced-backed claims. In general, there is a tendency to think that if an intelligent person is good at one thing, they are good at many other things that require intelligence. What is different now is that trillion-dollar companies and large swathes of the global economy now depend on this being true of artificial intelligence. Advertisement To be clear, I think we must now admit that AI is better at solving open mathematical problems than any human, and that this has happened faster than anyone ever expected. When I first saw the news in September that the Navier-Stokes problem had been solved by OpenAI, I felt stunned. We had entered a new world. With the announcement of the Riemann hypothesis proof this week, I felt sick and had to go and have a lie-down. These were intellectual Everests I have marvelled at since my teenage years, conquered by a machine far sooner than anyone expected. You may have read my recent piece forecasting the future in 2096 – an early draft had a line, later removed, about three Millennium Prize Problems being solved by AI in the 2030s. We’ve had two this year alone. But maths isn’t biology. Yes, we have seen advances like AlphaFold, Deepmind’s AI that can predict the structure of proteins, but this is biology at its most mathematical, a computational puzzle. True advances in biology and medicine require studying cells, animals and people, all of which can be frustratingly illogical and uncooperative. Amodei admitted as much in 2024, writing that “the main challenges with directly applying intelligence to biology are data, the speed of the physical world, and intrinsic complexity”. You can imagine mitigations here – AI-directed robotic labs, for example – but it doesn’t seem like we should expect massive speed leaps in capability comparable to those seen in mathematics. There isn’t an easy way to confirm that a biological discovery is correct, in the manner that the computer code Lean allows for mathematics. Worse still are claims that AI will “solve climate change”. For Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, this came as a throwaway comment in a 2024 essay : “Although it will happen incrementally, astounding triumphs – fixing the climate, establishing a space colony, and the discovery of all of physics – will eventually become commonplace.” But we already know the solution to climate change: reduce greenhouse gas emissions to net zero and the warming will stop. The blockers to doing so, as demonstrated by the recent failure of the COP31 climate summit, are political, not technological. Even if AI were to produce a blueprint for a perfectly functioning nuclear fusion reactor tomorrow, we would still have to build thousands of them across the globe in the next decade or so to avoid the most catastrophic warming effects. In the past decade, we have built 60 nuclear fission reactors, a technology we understand far better than an as-yet-mythical fusion power plant. Again, you can see how AI might offer some improvements, but not enough to counteract our fossil fuel use. It is important for me to have some humility here, because one thing AI’s breakthroughs in mathematics this year has underlined for me is the need to change my mind when the evidence changes. I started that process with the early signs of AI progress in maths, but didn’t update my beliefs fast enough – though, to be fair to myself, neither did almost everyone else, including leading mathematicians such as Terence Tao, who, just weeks ago, said he didn’t expect the Riemann hypothesis to be solved by AI until 2050. For that reason, I am on the lookout for early signs that AI success in biology is shifting. That could include an AI-designed drug proving useful in people – for example, Rentosertib, a leading candidate, is now undergoing a phase III trial as a treatment for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a type of lung disease. The trial is expected to conclude in 2029, so we’re talking years of wait for any results. If the drug succeeds, that doesn’t necessarily provide a way for any other AI drug candidates to succeed, and the painfully slow process of molecule selection, animal testing and human trials is still hard to speed up. If I’m forced to make a prediction, I can fairly confidently state that we will see yet more advances in AI maths in 2027. I also expect that we will see some completely unexpected results in other fields as well. But solving biology? Ending climate change? Defeating disease? These still feel, for now, like science fiction. AI refutes 30-year-old mathematical assumption in computer science Further AI reading AI maths has become a spectator sport, thanks to a website dedicated to tracking agents attempting to solve the P vs NP problem, one of the remaining huge open problems in mathematics ( see my explanation of it here ). I don’t expect this approach to work – the models being used here are consumer ones, rather than the internal frontier models the AI firms have used for the big maths results so far. As if to illustrate this, both OpenAI and Anthropic have released, with little fanfare, solutions to the VP vs VNP problem. This is a lesser version of the P vs NP problem, and doesn’t necessarily help us get any closer to solving its big brother. And speaking of internal models, Axios reports that both Anthropic and OpenAI employees are concerned that their internal models are so powerful that they can’t safely be released. Take this with a big pinch of salt – Anthropic said the same about its Mythos model due to its cybersecurity abilities, then later released its Fable model, which is essentially just Mythos with some added guardrails. And don’t forget that, way back in the mists of 2019, OpenAI said that GPT-2 would be too dangerous to release. Today, you can run far more capable models on a smartphone, and no one finds that dangerous. Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO after a mere 11 days away following a scandal about his admitted affair with an alleged Chinese spy. For a reminder of why Nvidia is so important to the AI industry, see my previous column. A UN conference has failed to agree to a ban on autonomous weapons, as my colleague Matthew Sparkes predicted last week.
summary: AI Solves Riemann Hypothesis and Navier-Stokes, Raising Questions About Limits.
author: New Scientist

title: Ultracold atom experiment may rule out quantum theory interpretations
content: Standard quantum theory finds it difficult to predict the time a particle takes to travel between two points. Researchers propose that an experiment using ultracold atoms could test the theory’s predictions and potentially eliminate certain interpretations of quantum mechanics.
summary: Standard quantum theory struggles to predict how long a particle takes to travel between two points. An experiment with ultracold atoms could help rule out some interpretations.
author: New Scientist

title: Kidney protein that blocks excess phosphate may curb blood vessel aging
content: Researchers have identified a kidney protein that blocks excess phosphate from building up in the blood, a process that can turn flexible blood vessels rigid. In animal studies, lacking the protein sped up vascular aging and shortened lifespan, while lowering dietary phosphate reduced the damage. The findings suggest a link between phosphate intake, this kidney protein and blood‑vessel aging.
summary: Researchers identified a kidney protein that prevents excess phosphate from accumulating in the blood and stiffening vessels. In animal models, deficiency of the protein accelerated vascular aging and shortened lifespan, while reducing dietary phosphate lessened the damage.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists map hidden cave systems beneath Nullarbor Plain after solving trench mystery
content: Scientists have identified the cause of unusual trenches across Australia’s Nullarbor Plain as the gradual upward collapse of deeply buried cave systems over millions of years. The finding reveals an extensive hidden subterranean landscape and may guide researchers toward unexplored caves that could hold ancient environmental records and unusual life forms.
summary: Scientists have solved the mystery of strange trenches scattered across Australia’s vast Nullarbor Plain, revealing an extensive hidden world beneath the surface. The trenches are created as deeply buried cave systems slowly collapse upward over millions of years, and the discovery could help researchers locate unexplored caves with ancient environmental records and unusual life forms.
author: Science Daily

title: Study warns treating loneliness as medical condition may overlook social roots
content: Loneliness has been linked to a roughly 30 percent increase in the risk of premature death, according to previous research. A new study cautions that framing loneliness primarily as a medical condition may divert attention from its underlying social origins. The researchers suggest that, although healthcare professionals can provide support, durable remedies are likely to involve rebuilding communities and fundamentally altering how people live and work.
summary: Loneliness is linked to about a 30% higher risk of premature death. A new study says treating it as a medical condition could distract from deeper social causes, and lasting solutions may require rebuilding communities and changing how people live and work.
author: Science Daily

title: Men twice as likely as women to ignore conversation while multitasking, study finds
content: Researchers report that men and women are similarly capable of multitasking, but men are more than twice as likely to ignore conversation while handling multiple tasks. This disparity, they suggest, may help explain the common perception that women are better multitaskers.
summary: Men and women appear similarly capable of multitasking. However, men are more than twice as likely to ignore conversation while juggling multiple activities, a difference researchers say may explain why women are widely perceived as better multitaskers.
author: Science Daily

title: 345-million-year-old fossil reidentified as aquatic creature after X‑ray scan
content: A well‑known fossil dated to 345 million years ago has been reinterpreted after advanced X‑ray imaging uncovered hidden gills and thousands of tiny teeth. The new evidence shows the specimen was a primitive aquatic or amphibious animal, not the early reptile that scientists had identified for decades. The findings indicate that some traits previously thought to have originated in terrestrial vertebrates actually evolved while the animals were still dependent on water.
summary: Advanced X‑ray imaging of a famous 345‑million‑year‑old fossil revealed hidden gills and thousands of tiny teeth. The specimen is now interpreted as a primitive aquatic or amphibious animal rather than an early reptile, suggesting some land‑adaptations evolved in water‑dependent species.
author: Science Daily

title: Omega-3 and low-dose aspirin match antibiotics for severe gum disease
content: A study found that adding a combination of omega‑3 fatty acids and low‑dose aspirin to standard therapy for severe gum disease produced results comparable to those achieved with antibiotics. The benefits continued long after the supplements were stopped, suggesting the regimen could serve as an alternative for some patients and help lower dependence on antibiotics.
summary: A combination of omega-3 and low-dose aspirin produced results comparable to antibiotics when used alongside standard treatment for severe gum disease. The benefits persisted long after supplementation ended, suggesting an alternative that could reduce reliance on antibiotics.
author: Science Daily

title: Resolution Island designated historic sanctuary for kiwi and kākāpō
content: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Seeking Refuge on Resolution… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search In the late 1800s, wildlife conservationists in New Zealand were recognizing how predators such as stoats, brought to the country to control other nonnative animal populations, were becoming a threat to native birds. Naturalists at the time surmised that some of the nation’s islands could serve as sanctuaries where endemic species could persist, free from the voracious newcomers. Resolution Island, located in the Fiordland region along the rugged southwest edge of New Zealand’s South Island, was one of the first eyed for this purpose. Conservationist Thomas Henry Potts proposed in 1872 that the island could be a place where “wingless species, and birds of feeble powers of flight, might there find a refuge for some of their representatives.” So began an early systematic effort to protect kiwi, kākāpō, and other native birds on Resolution Island, the largest of the approximately 90 islands in Fiordland National Park. This image, acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on December 12, 2025, shows the island’s setting amid a landscape of steep-sided valleys carved by glaciers and now inundated by the ocean. The uninhabited island rises from sea level to the summit of Mount Clerke at 1,069 meters (3,507 feet). Its diverse habitats and vegetation communities range from bogs and wetlands near the coast to widespread podocarp forests at middle elevations to tussock grasslands in the subalpine and alpine areas. Offshore, the Taumoana (Five Fingers Peninsula) Marine Reserve protects estuarine and wave-exposed rocky reef habitats at the entrance to Dusky Sound, east of Five Fingers Peninsula. Farther into the sound, Pigeon Island was the onetime home of Richard Henry, who was named caretaker of Resolution Island after it was designated a reserve in 1891. In what some have called a “ landmark effort,” Henry spent years transporting more than 700 birds, mostly kiwi and kākāpō, by rowboat to Resolution and other would-be island sanctuaries nearby. In 1900, however, people began spotting mustelids on Resolution. It turns out the island is within swimming distance for animals such as stoats. Henry was intent on trapping the interlopers but eventually abandoned the project and moved on to caretaking work on another island. The spirit of his efforts lives on, though. A Department of Conservation program started in 2008 aims to control stoat populations and bolster native species on Resolution. title: APOD Nov 26 2026: Milky Way arches over Brazil’s Lençóis Maranhenses
content: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 26 – Eye… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Eye in the Sky: The Milky Way over Lençóis Explanation: Beauty is in the eye of the beholder. And there is much to behold in today’s featured image. The Milky Way shines bright in the sky of Brazil, over the white sand dunes and dark lagoons of Lençóis Maranhenses National Park. We can see different parts of the Milky Way as it apparently rotates in the sky every night and throughout the year. This composite image was taken later in the night in July from a latitude of approximately 2º south. It shows some prominent Milky Way features, such as dark dust lanes and colorful nebulas. But does the Galaxy really appear arched like a rainbow in the sky? No, this is an artifact of a picture taken with a wide-angle lens. As the Galaxy was artfully framed by the photographer, it matches the contour of the dark lagoon creating the illusion of a cosmic eye, half in space and half on the ground. Is this eye in the sky looking back at you? Tomorrow’s picture: what’s next?
